(Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October."There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds."I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness."And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sue Kim (right) followed Lisa for a year, as she launched her solo career during a break in Blackpink's activitiesThe incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head"."To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece."You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says."And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa put aside scandal and online death threats to put on one of the standout performances of 2025's Coachella Music FestivalImage source, Sony Music VisionImage caption, The documentary captures Lisa's joy - and relief - after she pulled off the hour-long showThe film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships."I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US."Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim."In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat."Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpink are one of K-pop's biggest bands, with hits like Whistle, How You Like That and Kill This LoveThe potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.Kim says that began to change as they filmed."I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career."Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview."And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."Image source, Fabio Lovino / HBOImage caption, The singer made her acting debut in season three of The White Lotus, filmed on location in her home countryKim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule."But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted."It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim."I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lisa won the award for best pop act at this year's MTV Awards, becoming the first K-pop star to lift the trophyIn the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised."Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says."She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power."That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'."So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."Related topicsFilmK-popBLACKPINKMusicMore on this storyBlackpink: K-pop band make 'epic Wembley dream' come truePublished16 August 2025From Squid Game to Blackpink, how South Korea became a culture powerhousePublished28 December 2024Blackpink star Lisa joins White Lotus castPublished13 February 2024

title: Myanmar's young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to the army
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductionsByGavin Butler and BBC Burmese Published10 October 2026You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.But Zaw Min has no choice."I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time."People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.Image source, Telegram/@pyithusittImage caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscripted by the junta since early 2024Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions."Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.They said they had no comment on the matter.With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025. Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law. "In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.Figure caption, Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time."We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities. When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription."[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls."If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward."I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousinIn the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.She does not know where her husband is now.Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says."Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison. BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful."Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says. "They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."Image source, BBC BurmeseImage caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo WaiWhile conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."Related topicsMyanmarAsiaMilitaryMore on this storyMillions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?Published30 JulyFrom behind bars, Aung San Suu Kyi casts a long shadow over MyanmarPublished14 JanuarySoldier-spies in Myanmar help pro-democracy rebels make crucial gainsPublished20 December 2024The college scam that promised students fleeing war a new life in FinlandPublished12 June

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila FlynnSenior US reporterPublished10 October 2026They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.Image source, FPG/Staff/GettyImage caption, Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the USA little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed."People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked."I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%."It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Figure caption, Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa PikeSonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream."What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution."I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University."Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"Figure caption, Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US."This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people.""I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."Related topicsUnited StatesKentuckyMore on this storyWho is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution onlinePublished1 day agoFort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestreamPublished2 days agoI've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike'sPublished2 October

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
content: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentPublished10 October 2026Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence."At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from CroatiaGermany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.But he is a civilian.Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."Croatia is a different matter.Political ripplesThe implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further."I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."First in the dockSerhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.They are not saying, though.And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.Related topicsUkraineGermanyWar in UkraineMore on the Nord Stream blastsUkrainian man arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline blastsPublished19 AugustSabotage behind Nord Stream gas leaks, says EUPublished28 September 2022A journey to the site of the Nord Stream explosionsPublished18 November 2022

title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
content: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?CloseUS President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.More on this story.SubsectionWorldPublished1 hour agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsDonald TrumpFollow Donald Trumpclose panelYou are now following Donald TrumpUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Volodymyr ZelenskyFollow Volodymyr Zelenskyclose panelYou are now following Volodymyr ZelenskyUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Vladimir PutinFollow Vladimir Putinclose panelYou are now following Vladimir PutinUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.War in UkraineFollow War in Ukraineclose panelYou are now following War in UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
content: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalBuildings swept away as flash floods hit central NepalCloseA flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal. The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed. It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river. Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.More on this story.SubsectionAsiaPublished12 hours agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsNepalFollow Nepalclose panelYou are now following NepalUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.FloodsFollow Floodsclose panelYou are now following FloodsUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi
content: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiWhy have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in DelhiCloseProtesters were heard slamming on bus windows following their detention during an anti-government demonstration called by The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi. The CJP shared a video on social media showing its founder Abhijeet Dipke being detained with other leaders shortly after landing in the capital. The movement started in May after India's Chief Justice likened some unemployed young people to "cockroaches". Delhi police denied permission for the demonstration to take place, with tens of thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. But the CJP had insisted it would go ahead. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri, on the ground in Delhi, explains what the latest protest is about.More on this story. title: Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
content: Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpWatch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpCloseUS President Donald Trump has called for new leadership in Ukraine, criticising President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries."It's time for Ukraine to get a new president" he told reporters. On Friday Trump announced a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, a deal Zelensky described as "a gift" to President Putin.Read more about the rising tensions between the US and Ukraine.SubsectionWorldPublished1 day agoShareclose panelShare pageCopy linkAbout sharingRelated topicsDonald TrumpFollow Donald Trumpclose panelYou are now following Donald TrumpUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.War in UkraineFollow War in Ukraineclose panelYou are now following War in UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Volodymyr ZelenskyFollow Volodymyr Zelenskyclose panelYou are now following Volodymyr ZelenskyUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.United StatesFollow United Statesclose panelYou are now following United StatesUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.RussiaFollow Russiaclose panelYou are now following RussiaUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.UkraineFollow Ukraineclose panelYou are now following UkraineUpdates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage.Read description

title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
content: Image source, Getty ImagesByTinshui YeungPublished11 October 2026Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.Figure caption, Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia"."Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.The BBC has asked the White House for further details.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region."All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.Image source, Telegram/CrimeanwindImage caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 AugustEarlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports."Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.Related topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyWar in UkraineMore on this story'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel dealPublished22 hours agoTrump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to PutinPublished1 day agoRussian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surgePublished3 days ago

title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
content: Figure caption, WATCH: The father and son on opposite sides of Alberta’s separation referendumByJames FitzGeraldPublished19 October 2026, 10:24 BSTUpdated 17 minutes agoPeople in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada. The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive. Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said. Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"Why is Alberta voting to separate from Canada, and how likely is it to happen?Published5 hours agoThe separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. They are both members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa.Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, they argue. They say Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada.Chris Scott, founder of pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the poll that the campaign had already achieved some of its goals, regardless of what happened on Monday. "The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue," he said. "What's started can't be stopped now," he added.Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt. They warn that the uncertainty - which they liken to the UK's Brexit vote to leave the European Union in 2016 - would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province.Pro-independence voters told the BBC in Edmonton over the weekend that they feel their voice is not heard in Ottawa, the national capital. "We really need to send a message to Ottawa, " said Jennifer Trudeau, who calls herself a sovereigntist. She said she did not want a full divorce from Canada, but believes the province needs to "assert its rights". At a separate unity rally in Edmonton, people told the BBC that they were proud Albertans but felt it was better to keep the country together. "Alberta is a strong province, but it is important that it stays within a united Canada," said Michele Jackson. "That is critical to me. I am Canadian 100%." Micah Sellers called the question about whether the province should pursue independence "ridiculous". "It's a waste of money," he said. "It's a distraction from real issues in Alberta and in Canada. I think if we're going to be asked, everyone should vote to remain." Carney has called on voters to deliver a decisive vote against separation. Speaking at a rally on Thursday, he warned that the stakes were high. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about his country's ongoing trade war with the United States.Alongside the separation question, Albertans will vote on nine other issues - a number of which focus on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system.Hundreds of thousands of people had voted early by post ahead of Monday, and early figures suggested a strong voter turnout. The province's election officials will count the ballots by hand, and have 48 hours to complete the task - starting from no earlier than 20:00 local time on Monday (02:00 GMT on Tuesday).The key question, on separation, will be counted in its entirety first. Officials have said results should be available in the early hours of Tuesday.Figure caption, Watch: 'I worry about the Brexit effect' - Albertans weigh in on independence from CanadaRelated topicsCanadaAlbertaMark CarneyMore on this storyCould Alberta's vote on independence be Canada's Brexit moment? title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie faces verdict on 191 murder charges in Kenya
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie operated his church for 16 years, attracting thousands of followersByThomas MukhwanaAfrica correspondent, Reporting fromShakaholaPublished19 October 2026, 04:44 BSTUpdated 3 hours agoA Kenyan judge has started to deliver a verdict in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children.His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Image source, Salim KarisaImage caption, Salim Karisa was paid about $8 a day to dig up dozens of bodiesAlthough many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."Stephen Mwiti, 48, recounted losing all six of his children to the cult and seeing "many bald women and tens of children" surrounding Mackenzie in his house when he went to confront him. Mackenzie forbade make-up and hairstyles, so told women to shave off their hair or keep it unkempt.Mwiti's former wife is one of those accused alongside Mackenzie."If I met Pastor Mackenzie today, one of us will have to die," told the BBC. Image source, Mohamed Madi / BBCImage caption, Stephen Mwiti says his six children died in the forest"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel.""This little thing here was the start of all my misery," Mwiti said as he pointed at a dusty TV and cable box in his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola. It was from that TV that Mackenzie's doctrine made it to his home.The pastor established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya.His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".Image caption, This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermonsMackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning." The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."Image caption, Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good manIn the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, 190 victims of the 191 Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children. Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."More about Kenya's cult from the BBC:'I fear for my sons': Mother awaits DNA results on remains linked to Kenya's starvation cultPublished31 August 2025What did the Kenyan starvation cult leader preach?Published10 May 2023Kenya cult targeted children to starve first - pastorPublished14 May 2023The mother who fled a death cult to save her childrenPublished18 May 2023Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, external, on Facebook at BBC Africa, external or on Instagram at bbcafrica, externalRelated topicsKenyaReligionCultsAfricaBBC Africa podcastsFocus on AfricaThis Is Africa

title: World Food Programme forced to cut aid to Gaza due to funding shortages
content: Image caption, Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cutsByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondent, Reporting fromJerusalemPublished8 hours agoOne of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.Image caption, Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster""It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat.""This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."Image caption, Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-MawasiAlready, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.Image caption, Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed expertsFamilies currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets."The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food."It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."Image caption, Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cookingHumanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September. The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.Related topicsPalestinian territoriesIsrael-Gaza warMore on this story'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stallsPublished8 OctoberGirl has multiple surgeries to control infections after strike in GazaPublished30 SeptemberReports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency findsPublished23 SeptemberFamilies' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in GazaPublished19 August'Digital lifeline' - Gaza tech workers give glimpse of possible futurePublished4 August

title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
content: Image source, ReutersByJack Burgess and Toby MannPublished18 October 2026Updated 19 October 2026 00:20 BSTUS President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on FridayZelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.Related topicsWar in UkraineDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyVladimir PutinMore on this storyTrump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifiesPublished1 day agoZelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'Published2 days agoRussia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resumePublished3 days ago

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate
content: Image source, Sebastião Moreira EPAImage caption, Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are competing for the presidency in a run-off election due on SundayByVanessa Buschschlüter, Latin America online editor and Mariana Schreiber, BBC News Brasil in BrasiliaPublished2 hours agoBrazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters. But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula. Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election. The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time". Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments. "The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin". Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia". Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).Image source, Sebastião Moreira/EPAImage caption, Bolsonaro had highlighted the initials for the Workers' Party on his hand"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese. Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power. He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election loomsPublished2 days agoBrazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for LulaPublished4 days agoRight-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round of Brazil electionPublished6 OctoberRelated topicsBrazilLuiz Inacio Lula da SilvaJair Bolsonaro

title: Meloni calls emergency meeting after violent clashes in Milan
content: Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 200 people were arrested across the weekend, according to Italian mediaByHafsa KhalilPublished2 hours agoItalian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers. "To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured. Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting."Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.Related topicsItalyEuropeGiorgia MeloniMore on this storyBurnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and lootingPublished1 day agoKatya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violencePublished6 hours ago

title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Two Bangladeshi nationals were executed over an "indecent act" in a mosque, Saudi authorities sayByKoh EwePublished5 hours agoBangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam. The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.Related topicsMeccaSaudi ArabiaAsiaMiddle EastBangladesh

title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
content: Figure caption, Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fireByPaulin KolaPublished4 hours agoThe fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds."The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition.
