Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military basePublished2 hours agoTributes are being paid to the servicemen who died. Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."Figure caption, Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayorIn account of Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time"."I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said.According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.Related topicsCanadaAlbertaMilitaryMark Carney

title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
content: Image source, Robert KaberaImage caption, Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singerPublished19 October 2026, 14:13 BSTUpdated 20 minutes agoA former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety."It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.Reacting to news of his murder, the opposition Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics."Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.More about Rwanda from the BBC:Why Rwanda's deal for F1 race remains controversialPublished4 days agoEx-head of Rwanda's presidential guard dies in jail 12 years after his arrestPublished26 AugustLand of safety - or fear? Why Rwanda divides opinionPublished14 April 2022Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, external, on Facebook at BBC Africa, external or on Instagram at bbcafrica, externalRelated topicsAfricaUgandaPaul KagameRwandaBBC Africa podcastsFocus on AfricaThis Is Africa

title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
content: Image source, Archaeological Legacy InstituteImage caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object, which some had hypothesised could have been Amelia Earhart's plane, in a lagoon on NikumaroroByJacob PhillipsPublished4 hours agoResearchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters."This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object."The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world.She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea.Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California.But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel.One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island.They spent four days onshore investigating the site.Related topicsPacific OceanKiribatiMore on this storyExpedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote islandPublished10 October

title: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai
content: Figure caption, Watch: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in MumbaiByNikita YadavBBC News, DelhiPublished19 October 2026, 02:50 BSTUpdated 6 hours agoPolice in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds.The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening while he was in a car leaving a football ground in Juhu suburb. Videos showed at least two men firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of Shroff's car while it was moving slowly past a crowd.Two people, including Shroff's driver, were injured, according to the police. Three people were detained in Rajasthan on Monday in connection with the incident, the police said. The attack has sent shockwaves through Bollywood, with celebrities raising concerns about Shroff's safety. Several actors and political figures in Mumbai have been targeted by gunmen in recent years.Shroff, the son of veteran Bollywood actor Jackie Shroff, made his film debut with Heropanti in 2014. He has appeared in many action films, and is popular with fans for his dancing and martial arts skills.He is also a professional footballer and made his debut for Mumbay FC in October 2024 in a regional tournament. He was leaving the football ground after his regular practice session when the attack happenedEknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state of which Mumbai is the capital, visited Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor had been left "shaken" by the attack."These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," Shinde said.In a photograph showing Shroff with Shinde, the actor is seen shirtless with some bandages on his upper body. It's not clear yet what injuries he sustained.Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis described the incident as "serious and condemnable", and said that the police would arrest some people "very soon".He said he had told Shroff that he should not worry, and that the government would ensure his "complete safety".Rajasthan police said two of the three suspects detained were from the northern states of Haryana and Bihar and had been living in Mumbai for the past few years. The third suspect is a minor.They are expected to be handed over to Mumbai Police later in the day.Image source, ANIImage caption, Tiger Shroff (left) was seen with bandages on his upper body when Maharashtra deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde visited him at his house after the shooting attemptThe All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA), a large union, condemned the attack, alleging that gangsters were deliberately targeting people in the film industry to create an "atmosphere of fear" and extort money from celebrities.In a statement, the association criticised the government and police for failing to prevent such attacks. It called for strict action against those responsible and better security for film industry workers and their families.The association also said the incident was a reminder of the 1990s, when criminal gangs wielded considerable influence in the city. It said that the film industry should not have to "work under the shadow of fear".Police have not yet confirmed who was behind the shooting. But Indian media reports have been widely reporting that an audio clip has surfaced in which a man claiming to be linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang says he is responsible.Bishnoi is currently lodged in a high-security prison in Gujarat state in connection with several high-profile cases.The authenticity of the recording and the man's claims have not been independently verified and police have not confirmed the gang's involvement yet.But the reports have brought the Bishnoi gang back into the headlines.In 2024, police arrested two people allegedly linked to the Bishnoi gang for a gun attack that targeted the home of Bollywood superstar Salman Khan.That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai. His murder, in a bustling neighbourhood in Mumbai, was also reportedly linked to people associated with the Bishnoi gang.Additional reporting by BBC MarathiRelated topicsIndiaMumbaiBollywoodAsia

title: Bomb threat forces Tel Aviv to Vienna flight to land in Bulgaria
content: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, An Austrian Airlines jet similar to the one diverted to BulgariaByHarry Sekulich and Toby MannPublished19 October 2026, 03:41 BSTUpdated 7 hours agoAn Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat.The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement.The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the statement said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made.Austrian Airlines confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the BBC there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet.Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia.Austrian Airlines confirmed that no threat was found and the flight finished its journey to Vienna with all passengers on board.Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later.Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.Related topicsAviation safetyIsraelAviation accidents and incidentsAustriaLufthansaMore on this story'I was not going to let others die' - pilot of Flydubai flight describes cockpit attack by co-pilotPublished2 OctoberFlydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE saysPublished10 October

title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
content: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichael Race, Business reporter and Simon Jack, Business editorPublished19 October 2026, 00:28 BSTThe boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures."Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia."Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help."I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years"."Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids."The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks.""Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history"."We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."Related topicsWar in UkraineSteel industryEuropean UnionTradeUkraineInternational Business

title: Musk and Anthropic pledge share giveaways
content: Image source, ReutersByPeter Hoskins and Michael Race, Business reportersPublished19 October 2026, 03:41 BSTUpdated 4 hours agoElon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed. In a post on social media,, external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity."I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".Related topicsInternational BusinessArtificial intelligenceElon MuskSpaceXCompaniesMore on this storyWhy are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?Published17 SeptemberAnthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systemsPublished9 October

title: Jordon Steele-John: Australian senator denies claims of misconduct against women
content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against womenByLana LamSydneyPublished19 October 2026, 02:32 BSTUpdated 9 hours agoAn Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.A spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader still believed "leave is appropriate under the circumstances" and taking leave would not influence the internal party investigation.Related topicsAustralia

title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
content: Figure caption, Watch: Police 'lost control' in French cities, interior minister saysByKatya AdlerEurope editor, Reporting fromParisPublished19 October 2026, 05:16 BSTUpdated 6 hours agoFrance's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez tried to hand in his resignation, the Élysée Palace (French President Macron's HQ) announced on Monday morning. But instead, Macron has asked him to examine how to make France's streets safer and to bring the perpetrators of the weekend violence to justice.Over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated on Saturday against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.Interior Minister Nuñez has been accused by political opponents, some trade unions and on social media forums for being ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened."Things are dark in the City of Light" - the nickname for Paris - was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.Macron's speech has been roundly criticised in the French media for lacking concrete detail.How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? That is how these demonstrations started in the first place, last month.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekendOn Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.The president has apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Macron is widely viewed in France as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out.There is a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alightMany passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility."While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.France is holding its breath.Related topicsEmmanuel MacronFranceFrench politicsMore on this storyMacron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across FrancePublished8 hours agoBurnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and lootingPublished1 day agoAre student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?Published3 days ago

title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
content: Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videosByMonica GarnseyBBC Eye Published19 October 2026, 01:06 BSTTwo Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his carThere have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineTwo men tell of secret operations inside Russia.Watch on iPlayerListen to the Podcast on BBC Sounds.If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineIvan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome."At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war... Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets."When these [drone] components are combined... it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers "You will get a file... from me or a colleague... with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets."This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live... Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live."In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals."As a rule... we also check the data [on that person]... Only after that we say whether we work or not."But he argued that his team's actions were justified."I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine... to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.Foma did his own digging on Ivan.After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too."The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.Foma has the same rule for his operatives."As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats... leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work."Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travelMamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him."You go to a third country... where [Ukraine's] agents meet you... and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag."There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes... and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work."Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change."Putin won't live forever," he said.Related topicsWar in UkraineRussiaUkraineSpyingDrones

title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
content: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational correspondent, Columbus, OhioPublished18 October 2026Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicideThe few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood."This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars."You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic WaveExtraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.Watch on iPlayerImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanylImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.Recovery group offering hopeAt the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid."It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood ChurchImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same timeBoth in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose"."In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so."The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope DealersOverdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine."The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.Watch the documentary on YouTube, externalI meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear. "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening."In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters."Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in lettersIn August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moistureOutside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous"."Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics."The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."'A lot of people are struggling'Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.Additional reporting by Darren ConwayIf you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.Related topicsUnited StatesDrugs tradeDrug useFentanylHeroin

title: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
content: Image source, Vantor/BBCBySoram Cheon, BBC Korean and Aghnia Adzkia, East Asia Visual JournalismPublished17 October 2026An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size."In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in KalmaA South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.Image source, VantorImage caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told the Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is unclear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first."Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."Graphics by: Arvin SupriyadiRelated topicsKim Jong UnNorth KoreaMore on this storyWhy Kim Jong Un never talks about his mother - or her controversial bloodlinePublished28 JuneKim Jong Un was meant to be their only idol - then North Koreans discovered K-popPublished17 JulyCould Kim's teen daughter become North Korea's next leader?Published1 March

title: The uncertain future of Marineland's 30 rescued belugas
content: Image source, Toronto Star via Getty ImagesImage caption, Marineland was once an iconic Canadian attraction, known for its Everyone loves Marineland jingleByMax MatzaPublished17 October 2026Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio and even Valencia in Spain.Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago and Osorio felt the weight of the moment."This is the last one to happen and it's never going to happen again," he says.Figure caption, Watch: First beluga whales rescued from closed Marineland park arrive at new homes in the USDespite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has had the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appeared to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. About 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025, according to a tally by the Canadian Press.Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes following the death of its longtime owner.Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals that includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.Image source, Georgia AquariumImage caption, The Georgia aquarium took in two belugas: Balor and ZephyrMatlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales."If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement. In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".They said the remaining belugas show positive signs, including eating well. World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.As they cannot be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales."I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m).But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer."They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state. He adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks."It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity.Image source, The Whale Sanctuary Project/ Lori MarinoImage caption, The Whale Sanctuary Project is constructing a site off the coast of Nova ScotiaJason Jones, senior curator of animal wellbeing at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life"."Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so."Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, seven. They joined the four females already in their care.They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says."There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group." "They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Former Marineland trainer Phil Demers is an advocate for animal welfarePhil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who spoke to the BBC, says the end of Marineland is "bittersweet".He's grateful to see the facility shut down and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat.He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV."I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says.Related topicsCanadaWhalesAnimal rightsMarine lifeMore on this storyThirty belugas in Canada face being euthanised. Can they be saved?Published12 October 2025More whales are stranding. Now more people are needed to help themPublished10 MarchHow a Canadian walrus ended up in Abu DhabiPublished18 May 2023

title: French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right?
content: ListenListen (6 mins)SaveShare French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right? on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoMarine Le Pen, French far-right leader and member of parliament, who is running in the 2027 French presidential election for the National Rally, blows a kiss to the crowd during her speech in Henin-Beaumont, France, September 13, 2026 [Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters]By Shola LawalPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026As massive protests swept through cities across France over the weekend, degenerating into riots in many places, far-right politician Marine Le Pen has attempted to profit from the crisis ahead of the presidential election in April 2027.On Sunday, the leader of the National Rally party, or RN by its French initials, railed against President Emmanuel Macron’s handling of the crisis in a video statement, saying the outgoing centre-right leader no longer has any “credibility or authority” and that the country’s people were caught between his austerity “hammering” them on the one hand and “insurrectionary activists” on the left on the other.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?list 2 of 4‘Anger and shame’: Macron denounces France’s nationwide rioting, lootinglist 3 of 4France’s Macron declines minister’s resignation after violent protestslist 4 of 4What’s wrong with schools in France?end of listSchool protests in France erupted on September 21 in a poor borough of Paris as pupils demonstrated against dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages and tight class schedules. The demonstrations quickly spread across the country and coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s plans to cut public spending.Le Pen blamed the political left and “decades of immigration” to France for the looting and destruction that trailed the demonstrations, and presented her party as capable of restoring order — without offering any firm evidence to back up assertions that the rioting was led by immigrants.The politician is already far ahead in recent polls, and some say she is likely to be the next leader. Here’s what we know:Rubbish burns during clashes between protesters and police during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students’ grievances, in Paris, October 18, 2026 [Emma Da Silva/AP Photo]What happened over the weekend?Scenes of burned cars, vandalised and looted shops and defaced public buildings emerged from across France. Advertisement Some 550,000 people demonstrated on Saturday, according to the Ministry of the Interior, although protest organisers put the figure at 800,000. Protesters included students, union groups and supporters of the “yellow vests” movement, which protested against inflation back in 2018, at the start of Macron’s presidency.Although most marched peacefully, masked groups attacked city halls in several cities on Saturday, including the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, which was badly damaged.In Lyon, a tourist office was set ablaze.In Marseille, hooded individuals attacked a police station. The city has since banned protests.Looters also targeted hundreds of shops in several locations.In Paris, storefronts were shattered and broken glass littered the Place de la Republique. The Marianne statue, an important symbol of France, was partially dismantled. Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, but did not provide more details.Protesters and rights groups have accused police of using disproportionate force throughout the protests. Some 2,400 people were arrested by Sunday, officials said. Several police officers were injured.In a national address, Macron condemned rioters and accused far-left groups of attacking police and public buildings. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday that partial curfews would be imposed in some areas.How could the far right gain?Peter McPhee, a professor emeritus at the University of Montreal, described the protests as a “Christmas present” for Le Pen’s National Rally ahead of the presidential election.Le Pen said in a video statement protesters have “legitimate social grievances” but that Macron’s government was “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable” of addressing them.She criticised the administration’s controversial budget plans and promised to free the French from “Macronist toxic policies” while failing to mention that her party has also proposed strict spending cuts to bring down rising public debt.The politician, who is far ahead of other candidates in the polls, fuelled right-wing narratives spreading online that immigrants, not the French people, are instigating the protests, even as the grievances driving the agitation have intersected, with flag-carrying pro-Palestinian, environmental, feminist and anticolonial movements joining in.McPhee called Le Pen’s move “profoundly worrying”.“It is easy for Le Pen to make the link between the violent attacks on buildings and shops with African migrants because of the Palestinian and Algerian flags,” the professor said. “People in many parts of the world are attracted to simplistic, often racist, answers to economic and social problems.” Advertisement Analysts add that far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, or LFI, who has joined the protests, could also face backlash if anger grows over the destruction, further handing Le Pen a stronger platform.How did the far right gain ground after previous protests?Right-wing and centrist parties have historically gained after mass protests and disorder as people, fearing anarchy, vote for them.In May 1968, similar student-led protests erupted after millions of students and striking workers rallied against poor schooling conditions, increasing economic inequalities and stagnant wages.Left-wing communist and socialist political parties joined the protests and called for a revolution. Then-President Charles de Gaulle’s conservative government initially struggled to control the demonstrations, even escaping to a French base in West Germany for a few days as violence spiralled and the country ground to a standstill.However, the protest soon lost momentum amid the shutdown of public services. De Gaulle dissolved parliament and called for snap elections in June 1968, blaming the left for the violence and promising to restore order. His conservative Union for the Defence of the Republic party went on to win in an astounding landslide while left-wing parties lost more than half their seats.Again, during the 2018 “yellow vest” demonstrations, working-class protesters rallying against Macron’s government’s decision to raise taxes found support among Le Pen’s party, although the left wing also tried to ingratiate itself with the movement.Many of the movement’s supporters ended up voting for Le Pen’s party in the 2022 legislative elections to punish the Macron government, a move that still shapes the deeply divided parliament.
