title: Qatar warns global energy shockwaves from Iran war have yet to peak
content: ListenListen (4 mins)SaveShare Qatar warns global energy shockwaves from Iran war have yet to peak on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoQatar's Deputy Prime MInister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday, October 19, 2026 [Screen grab/Global Security Forum]By Usaid SiddiquiPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026Doha, Qatar — Qatar’s deputy prime minister has warned that global energy shockwaves from the US-Israel war on Iran have yet to reach their peak, raising concerns about further disruption to supplies, international trade and economic growth.Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who also serves as Minister of State for Defence Affairs, identified several threats facing Qatar and the wider Gulf, including risks to sovereignty and disruptions to energy supplies.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Iran’s president condemns environmental impact of war in Middle Eastlist 2 of 3How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm electionslist 3 of 3US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vesselsend of list“We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” he said, warning of further repercussions “in the coming days and months”.His remarks come amid continued instability in the Strait of Hormuz – a vital waterway for global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments – following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28, and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes across the region. Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan industrial complex in March damaged facilities, with repairs expected to take several years.“We were surprised,” Al Thani said when asked about the attack, adding that there had since been “a lot of discussion with Iran”.He said Qatar had drawn lessons from the strikes, “to make sure that all of our assets will be protected from any unexpected attack”.Al Thani also warned against imposing tolls on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.“Transit fees should not be applied,” he said, adding that uncertainty over the waterway would ultimately affect consumers worldwide. Advertisement ‘We never stop our communication’Despite the attacks, Al Thani said Qatar continued to maintain contact with Tehran.“We never stop our communication,” he said, adding that the two countries remained in touch at different levels despite their disagreements.He described Qatar’s relationship with Iran before the attacks as one of trust, pointing to their shared offshore gasfield and longstanding economic interests.Al Thani expressed hope that mediation efforts involving Qatar, Pakistan and Oman would help produce an agreement between the United States, Iran and other parties, including Israel.He said a sustainable settlement would require broader regional dialogue involving Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, Pakistan and Turkiye, in consultation with international allies.“We need to build this on trust,” he added.Al Thani also suggested developing economic ties with Iran to prevent future conflicts, citing cooperation between France and Germany following decades of hostilities.“Iran is our neighbour. We need to find ways to live with them,” he said.US defence tiesAl Thani also highlighted Qatar’s longstanding defence partnership with Washington, saying that “more than 90 percent” of attacks had been prevented through shared expertise and military capabilities developed over the past three to four decades.He said Qatar was continuing to develop Al Udeid airbase, which hosts US forces and military personnel from other partner countries.The base was itself targeted by Iran during the conflict, with Qatar reporting that it had shot down two Iranian warplanes during an attack in early March.Al Thani also announced plans for a new regional defence partnership, saying Qatar was prioritising several aspects including air defence, counter-drone measures and cybersecurity.“I’m happy to announce today also that soon we’re going to announce a new partnership,” he said, without naming the regional partners involved.The deputy prime minister stressed that Qatar’s mediation efforts did not diminish its commitment to defending its territory.“Mediation doesn’t mean that we should not be ready for any defensive action from our side,” he said.

title: How a grass fire at a Canadian military base killed four soldiers
content: ListenListen (5 mins)SaveShare How a grass fire at a Canadian military base killed four soldiers on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoA sign outside Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, Canada, October 18, 2026 [AFP]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026On Saturday morning, Canadian military officials at a base in Alberta province observed a grass fire that appeared sufficiently contained, allowing soldiers to conduct live-fire combat training. Then, the officials say, the wind shifted.In less than a minute, Canadian soldiers went from training drills to being engulfed in flames, said Major-General Wade Rutland, describing the incident that killed four soldiers and injured 39 people, 19 of them critically.“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” Rutland said at a news conference in Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, on Sunday.While the cause of the grass blaze remains unknown, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.So how did the grass fire spread so fast, and why is this base significant?Firefighters and emergency services close to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Wainwright, Alberta, October 18, 2026 [AFP]What is a grass fire?A grass fire spreads through dry grass, weeds, shrubs and other low-growing vegetation. Unlike forest fires that burn through trees and woodland, grass fires spread across open fields, grasslands and plains.They can move exceptionally quickly because dry grass ignites easily and provides a continuous source of fuel, and wind can play a pivotal role in how the fire develops.Strong winds push flames rapidly across open terrain, change their direction with little warning, and carry burning embers ahead of the main fire, potentially igniting new fires. Advertisement The uncertainty of winds makes grass fires difficult to predict and contain, particularly in dry conditions.They may burn for a shorter time than a forest fire, and while they are easier to contain, the speed at which they can spread in dry conditions can make them lethal.Grass fires can start naturally but can also be ignited by human activities, such as discarded cigarettes or equipment sparks.What happened at the base?The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, western Canada, about 210km (130 miles) southeast of Edmonton.The area lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees. The base is also one of the Canadian Army’s largest training centres and a key facility for preparing troops for operational deployment.About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire towards the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm, with gusts up to 100km/h (62mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.On Sunday, the Canadian media reported that the fire could have worsened after a gas facility was struck during a live firing exercise. However, the military later clarified that investigators do not believe any explosions were caused by oil or gas infrastructure.Firefighters continue to work close to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, October 18, 2026 [AFP]Were there initial warnings?Global News, a Canadian publication, reported that an armed forces memo obtained by it noted the fire risk was assessed as low for the scheduled live-ammunition exercise, greenlighting soldiers to train.However, Environment Canada had issued a strong-wind warning earlier that day, forecasting gusts of up to 100km/h in parts of Alberta.The memo also noted that blazes jumped a fire guard and spread outside the base, forcing the evacuation of one family home.“During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” the memo states. Advertisement Global News reported that the memo warned that the situation was “fluid” and the casualty figures “may change over time with ongoing assessments” of status.Why is the base significant?The Wainwright base is one of the country’s largest and most used military facilities, especially for training soldiers. It spans 609sq km (235sq miles) and is home to 25 weapons ranges.During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.

title: Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
content: ListenListen (4 mins)SaveShare Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoUkrainian officials have repeatedly said some ​Russian attacks on their capital, Kyiv, had occurred without warning [File: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied any suspension of intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington has resumed providing critical ⁠intelligence to help Kyiv defend against Russian missile strikes.“There has been no pause,” Rubio told reporters while on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday. “What [Zelenskyy] should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war.”Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’list 2 of 3Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edgelist 3 of 3Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy saysend of listUkraine has ⁠relied on US intelligence through Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, to detect the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities.Asked about a possible ‌meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to ⁠the more than four-year Ukraine war, ⁠Rubio said: “There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know ⁠whether it’s been finalised, but ⁠the president [Trump] ⁠has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia ‌to end.”The comments were made after Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme on Sunday, Zelenskyy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but was later “deblocked”.“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”Waiving sanctions on RussiaZelenskyy also said ‌other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine. Advertisement “If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course, we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand,” he said. Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia while accusing Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.He claimed that “Zelenskyy doesn’t care” about ending the conflict. “Frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him ... he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”Trump has temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing large quantities to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices.The US president also reiterated his accusation that Ukraine was purposefully targeting Russian refineries to try to hurt Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 midterm elections.Polling has suggested Trump’s party is heading for a likely defeat in the elections as many voters are upset by fuel costs, which have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke with Meet the Press after it ‌aired Zelenskyy’s interview, saying the Ukrainian president “presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must ‌win”.“The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement,” he said.Bessent slammed the claim that the US government was behind the slowing of the SpaceX satellite communications. “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” he said. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian missile attack ⁠killed ⁠a woman and wounded several people in the capital, Kyiv, overnight, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.The attack also damaged a metro station, a medical facility, an educational institution and a nonresidential building, according to the State Emergency Service.

title: For fifth straight week, NFL’s Azeez Al-Shaair honours Palestinian children
content: ListenListen (3 mins)SaveShare For fifth straight week, NFL’s Azeez Al-Shaair honours Palestinian children on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoLinebacker Azeez Al-Shaair warms up with Maryam Ghanem's name on his eyeblack before his team, the Houston Texans, NFL game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium in London, UK, October 18, 2026 [Kin Cheung/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026American football player Azeez Al-Shaair has honoured a Palestinian child for the fifth consecutive week by writing the name of Maryam Ghanem, a girl who was orphaned in Gaza last week, on his eyeblack for his team’s latest National Football League game.Al-Shaair carried Ghanem’s name on the black tape across his nose during the Houston Texans’ fixture against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium in London, United Kingdom, on Sunday.Ghanem is a two-and-a-half-year-old girl in Gaza who was forced to watch her mother burn alive after an Israeli strike hit their home in the Remal neighbourhood of Gaza City on Wednesday.[Screengrab/Instagram/a_train2_]Local journalists managed to rescue her after hearing her cries as flames engulfed her home in an apartment building that was struck early that morning. Ghanem was later identified as the sole survivor of her family.She was moved to hospital for treatment. “My hand hurts,” Ghanem said as she lay shell-shocked on a hospital bed, suffering from severe burns, and clutching her doll close to her.Maryam lost her father at the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and has now lost her mother as well.Israeli air strikes continue to pound Gaza regularly despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” in the besieged Strip. Al-Shaair has used his social media accounts and his eyeblack, a tape worn by athletes to reduce glare, to bring attention to the killings of Palestinians in the three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Advertisement The 29-year-old has been fined and has reportedly been threatened with removal from games, but he remains undeterred.The Black American Muslim player began his current NFL season by wearing the name of Hind Rajab on September 13.The five-year-old girl was killed in Gaza after Israeli soldiers opened fire on her family’s stranded car on January 29, 2024.Azeez Al-Shaair has been honouring Palestinian children for five weeks [Kin Cheung/AP Photo]The NFL fined him $11,491 for breaching the league’s code of conduct on players’ clothing and equipment during a match against the Buffalo Bills.However, basketball player Kyrie Irving stepped in and offered to pay the fine for Al-Shaair, who later confirmed that he had been in touch with the nine-time NBA All-Star.Al-Shaair brushed off talk of the fine while speaking to reporters last week. “It’s bigger to me; what’s a life worth? Is a life worth $11,000? No, I think it’s priceless,” he said.He has continued to raise awareness about the slain children by wearing a name, or combination of names, every Sunday.Prominent American Muslim scholar Omar Suleiman has repeatedly voiced his support for Al-Shaair.“My brother, who went to Jordan to be with Palestinian refugees this summer, who spends time with Palestinian children with missing limbs in Houston, who is using every week of his Pro Bowl NFL career to honour a Palestinian child despite the fines,” Suleiman wrote about Al-Shaair in a social media post last month.“In the sports and entertainment arenas run by many of the same types of people who run government, choose to be like Azeez Al-Shaair, Kyrie, and Macklemore.”The NFL’s fine on Al-Shaair came at a time when Robert Kraft, owner of the Boston-based team, the New England Patriots, confirmed that he pressured pop star Ed Sheeran to drop rapper Macklemore from his tour of the US.

title: Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government
content: ListenListen (8 mins)SaveShare Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoHezbollah supporters take to the streets in the southern suburbs of Beirut to protest against the trilateral agreement signed between the US, Israel and Lebanon in June 2026 [File: Ibrahim Amro/AFP]By Justin SalhaniPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026Beirut, Lebanon – Last week, Hezbollah announced it would provide financial support to families in Lebanon who had lost their homes in the latest war with Israel.Hezbollah has a long history of providing financial and other support for constituents and compensating those who have lost their homes to Israeli bombing. And while the group has historically received Iranian funding, it also has independent funding pathways allowing it to support members of its base, who are predominantly Lebanese Shia.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political realitylist 2 of 3Qatar announces ‘massive’ solar plant project in Lebanonlist 3 of 3The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahuend of listBut analysts said Hezbollah’s latest distribution drive, announced on October 13, is increasing pressure on the Lebanese government, which has sought to counter the group’s influence in the country.Last week, the government seized hundreds of kilogrammes of explosives linked to Hezbollah. Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said the stockpile belongs to the axis of resistance against Israel and demanded that it be handed back and those arrested be released.Meanwhile, Ali Damoush, the group’s executive council chairman, said on Tuesday Hezbollah would continue to support its constituents who have been on the front lines of the war with Israel.“At Hezbollah, and out of our religious and moral responsibility, we will continue to serve our people and make every possible effort to preserve their dignity and honour,” he said.Damoush said the payments were aimed at “displaced people and those whose homes had been destroyed or severely damaged to the point of becoming uninhabitable”.This follows a report by the Reuters news agency claiming that Iran had provided Hezbollah with $200m in an effort to ease the burden on Lebanon’s Shia population, after three years of devastating war with Israel. Advertisement At the height of the war, which began on October 8, 2023, there were as many as 1.2 million people displaced, with about 9,000 Lebanese killed.A United States Department of State official denied that Iran, under stringent economic pressure, was able to transfer the funds to its Lebanese ally.Nicholas Blanford, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera that the funds would be a huge boon to the group.“In general, this will help. Hezbollah is very sensitive towards the needs of their support base, the Shia community, and I think that’s one of the reasons why they haven’t gone back to fighting the Israelis,” he said. “The Iranians call the shots ultimately, but for Hezbollah I think there’s an awareness that they need to let their people breathe a little bit.”Supporters hold up Hezbollah flags and one bearing the image of the group’s slain leader Hassan Nasrallah during a ceremony held to mark the second anniversary of his killing in an Israeli strike, in Beirut, September 27, 2026 [AFP]Hezbollah paying out for the displacedIsrael intensified its war on Lebanon on March 2 this year, the second such escalation in less than two years.Hours earlier, Hezbollah had attacked Israel for the first time in more than a year after joint US-Israeli strikes on Tehran killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, an ally of the group. It also said Israel’s repeated violations of a 2024 ceasefire in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has traditionally had a strong presence, were another factor in opening up the war.In the following days, Israel reinvaded southern Lebanon, displacing more than a million people from their homes and killing about 4,300 since then. Israeli forces began their widespread aerial attacks on Lebanese villages and towns, which they claimed contained Hezbollah positions, with growing intensity.In June, a US-brokered trilateral framework was agreed between Israel and Lebanon. The goal was to have Israel withdraw from parts of southern Lebanon and have the Lebanese army deployed to disarm Hezbollah. Israel is yet to enter two of the first three pilot zone areas, where this programme was set to be unveiled.Since then, Israel has largely not withdrawn from the Lebanese territory but has entrenched what analysts believe is likely to become a long-term occupation, with more than 50 front-line villages and towns completely eradicated. Israel continues to demolish houses south of the so-called “Yellow Line”, in a tactic that has mirrored Israeli genocidal actions in Gaza. Advertisement Tens of thousands of people remain displaced, staying with relatives, renting apartments, or staying in hotels. Many had their livelihoods disrupted. In this context, Hezbollah has tried to step in and provide support for the displaced, most of whom are Shia Muslims and make up Hezbollah’s support base.A mourner grieves over one of the coffins during the funeral of Ali Samir al-Haj Hassan, a commander in Hezbollah’s elite Radwan Force, in Beirut’s southern suburb on August 16, 2026, after he was killed a day earlier along with his family members in a strike carried out by Israel’s military in the village of Ansar [AFP]Continued fundingThis is where the money from Iran reportedly comes in. However, analysts point out that Hezbollah has its own funding schemes, including financial support from the diaspora. Despite being heavily sanctioned, it is able to access money via domestic financial institutions or cryptocurrency.“It has access to funds from the state, wealthy individuals, various entities, companies and hospitals,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera.Hezbollah says its members have conducted surveys in Beirut’s southern suburbs and in southern Lebanon to assess the damage caused by the war. Families in Beirut and its suburbs whose homes were destroyed in the war will get $14,000 each; those outside the capital will receive $12,000. Financing will also be provided for furniture.The group said “everyone who has suffered harm in our country, regardless of their political position” will receive support. This suggests that even families who openly criticised the group for plunging the country into a disastrous war with Israel will also be eligible for payments.“Anyone who owns another home should, in solidarity with us, forgo the housing allowance, but will still receive the furniture allowance,” the group added.Hezbollah is widely acknowledged as Lebanon’s strongest political and military actor, but the group grew overconfident in the run-up to the October 7, 2023 attacks by Palestinian groups on Israel, analysts say.The political reality in Lebanon from that point changed, particularly after the 2024 Israeli intensification of its campaign against Hezbollah, which saw much of the group’s military leadership killed, including General Secretary Hassan Nasrallah.Such a blow has been difficult for the group and its constituents, who have borne much of the brunt of Israel’s assault on Lebanon.“It’s been a rough three years for them,” Atlantic Council’s Blanford said. “[The funding] will alleviate, to an extent, some people’s suffering.” Hezbollah’s announcement of support for those affected in the war is viewed by many as an attempt to maintain support on the ground.“Hezbollah knows that providing financial support and compensation to its on-the-ground population is one way to maintain its mass support,” Dania Arayssi, assistant director at New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera. “This is especially important because Hezbollah has seen a decline in mass support for it and a rise in mass frustration against this ongoing war.” Advertisement Challenge for BeirutBut the group’s efforts to pay off those who have suffered do not guarantee loyalty. Many in the Shia community have praised Hezbollah for the support they have received, but most say it is not enough to cover their expenses.“I’ve been hearing that there may be a problem between those that get compensation for destroyed homes and those with badly damaged homes who are going to get nothing,” Blanford said.Arayssi said Hezbollah’s latest move will also be a challenge for the Lebanese government, which has come under increasing Israeli and US pressure to take action against Hezbollah’s influence.Last Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio phoned Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun to press him on the issue of the Hezbollah explosives Lebanese forces had confiscated.“The Lebanese government is facing a real test and challenge to build and win the trust of the international community, and particularly the United States, against Hezbollah’s signalling attempts of rebuilding itself,” Arayssi said.“This funding and support for Hezbollah will likely make it harder to negotiate with Israel on the verification plan and even on the withdrawal from remaining territories, claiming that the government is failing to control its financial system.”

title: France’s Macron declines minister’s resignation after violent protests
content: ListenListen (3 mins)SaveShare France’s Macron declines minister’s resignation after violent protests on social mediashare-nodesSharefacebookxwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoForensic experts and police officers examine the burned Tourism Office in Lyon on October 18, 2026. a day after nationwide protests for educational reforms and against the high cost of living turned violent [Jeff Pachoud/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 19 Oct 202619 Oct 2026French ⁠President ⁠Emmanuel Macron has declined Interior Minister Laurent Nunez’s offer to resign ⁠after nationwide demonstrations by students protesting educational conditions and groups angry over the high cost of living turned into widespread riots and looting, the Elysee presidential office says.Macron said Nunez should stay in his position to ensure the chain of command is maintained within the police and security forces and asked the interior minister ⁠to establish new methods to deal with looters, the Elysee said in a statement on ⁠Monday.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and Francelist 2 of 4Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaoticlist 3 of 4Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?list 4 of 4‘Anger and shame’: Macron denounces France’s nationwide rioting, lootingend of listThe president also asked Nunez to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence”, the statement added.The Ministry of the Interior said more than 2,300 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured in protests on Saturday. Injuries were also reported among protesters, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.The nationwide demonstrations brought together students demanding better conditions in the French education system and residents protesting against the high cost of living and faltering public services.More than half a million people took part in the protests on Saturday. Looting, arson and damage to property occurred in many cities, with masked rioters attacking town halls, police stations and other government buildings. Nunez acknowledged on Monday that police “lost control” during the protests. Advertisement “On Saturday in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” Nunez said.Nunez acknowledged a “lack of anticipation” in the deployment of security forces on Saturday, saying their numbers were insufficient to deal with the large crowds of rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.He estimated that 60,000 law enforcement personnel were deployed across the country that day.“Given the damage that has been caused, it was only right that I should hand in my resignation,” Nunez said.Looting continued on Sunday, and Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, describing the scenes as “unbearable”.Nunez said about 350 people were arrested in Paris on Sunday and overnight.Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.The violent weekend demonstrations followed weeks of protests by high school students against overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and underinvestment in education, the biggest youth-led protest movement in the country in recent memory.

title: Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
content: Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks 19 October 2026 Climate and Environment Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people whose future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect our planet, the top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, said on Monday. The aim of the talks in the Armenian capital is to assess progress so far and build on an agreed blueprint for biodiversity protection known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted four years ago. Tweet URL “In 2022, 196 countries made commitments. But we are all accountable to each other and to future generations. What happens here in Yerevan matters. Billions of people whose lives are being upended by the impacts of biodiversity loss depend on progress being made here in the next two weeks,” said Executive Secretary of the UN Convention on Biodiversity, Astrid Schomaker.Tapping into indigenous ideasInsisting that “taking action for nature does work”, Ms. Schomaker called for the “untapped energy and ideas” of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth to contribute to the decisions made at the talks. “We need even greater engagement from cities, businesses and financial institutions...the science is clear. No nation, no economy, no society is immune from the impacts of biodiversity loss,” she said.The goals of the Convention include tackling the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, the unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species. Perhaps the Kunming-Montreal framework’s best-known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). To do this, national action plans must align with international goals, finance must match current needs and consumption and production should be in accord with “the finite resources of our planet”, Ms. Schomaker maintained.Why do these talks matter?A core aim of the Yerevan talks – also known as COP17, or the 17th Conference Of Parties – is “to turn commitments into measurable progress on the ground”, insisted Armenia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Paruyr Hovhannisyan.“We want COP17 to send a clear political signal that addressing biodiversity loss requires coordinated action by governments, international organizations, the private sector and civil society,” he told UN News. “This means strengthening implementation, mobilizing adequate resources, and improving monitoring and accountability.”Among the big issues governments will grapple with in Yerevan:Taking stock: Countries will conduct the very first global review of collective progress under the framework by presenting their national reports and updated national biodiversity strategies and action plans. This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed. Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Mr. Hovhannisyan.Making the Cali Fund work: This global financial mechanism established under the UN Convention on Biodiversity was agreed at COP16 in Cali, Colombia. Talks at Yerevan aim to advance practical arrangements for the fund, which was designed to collect funds from companies that use digital genetic data and redistribute these monies to protect biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples.Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results. Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.The meeting follows warnings from UN chief António Guterres in Yerevan on Friday that more than one million species face extinction.War on natureIn his call for an end to the “war on nature”, the UN Secretary-General appealed to governments, business and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations.“Every day, humankind saws another branch through the tree of life. Climate chaos, invasive species, overgrazing and overfishing, excessive fertilizers, pesticides, plastics and heavy metals, all these and more are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos,” he said.The UN chief warned that the world is edging ever closer towards becoming uninhabitable. But he also pointed to international biodiversity action agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Framework. It had inspired action worldwide, Mr. Guterres insisted, noting that since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.But “progress is uneven and far too slow” and countries risk falling “well short” of the goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by 2030, the UN chief said. ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film
content: Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film By Evgeniya Kleshcheva 18 October 2026 Culture and Education “I tell my kids I work in a time machine,” said Rhony Dostaly. In a basement beneath Lincoln Center, the media preservation engineer rescues moments from the past. “I go back in time, and I grab elements, and I make them available for people today.” He and his colleagues at the New York Public Library (NYPL) are working against the clock to preserve the contents of film, tape, discs and cylinders that hold more than a century of sound and moving images. The records are decaying, and the machines that can play them are disappearing. UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva Rhony Dostaly, Media Preservation Engineer. Learning from the pastFor Mr. Dostaly, it’s not just about technology. He has watched other people’s lives unfold through the archive. Harry Belafonte, the legendary American singer, actor, civil rights activist – and longtime UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador – filmed his family for decades, from teaching his son to ride a bike in Central Park to trips abroad. “I’ve actually seen his kids from toddlers all the way to adults,” Mr. Dostaly said. © UNICEF/Mariella Furrer UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador Harry Belafonte visits Nairobi, Kenya in 2004. Films of the African American civil rights leader Malcolm X’s travels, including footage from Mecca, moved him the most. “I’m the one who’s going to be making it available for everyone to see,” he remembered thinking.By looking through footage like this – he hopes – young people “will realize the importance of events that took place before they were here on Earth.”Cultural heritageNext door, Casey McNamara, a media preservation coordinator, bends over a reel of film with a jeweller’s loupe or magnifying glass, checking it frame by frame for tears, splices and shrinkage. On the white leader she has written “BHARATA NATYAM,” the name of one of the oldest Indian classical dance forms.Films may reach her “in a rusty tin, on an old projection reel, or in a rag box, in plastic bags.” Without the work she does, some collections “would remain mostly unseen.”The lab is part of NYPL’s Digital Collections Operations. Once digitized, most of the material will be accessible to anyone with a library card. “The tapes and the decks are no longer being manufactured, but the history needs to be preserved,” explained lab manager Shahed Dowlatshahi.Work like this is exactly the kind of project that the UN’s World Day for Audiovisual Heritage, marked annually on 27 October, is designed to highlight and assist.Preserving UN historyIn the audio room, Jeffrey Willens slides a 16-inch disc from a brown paper sleeve marked: A Year To Remember.The UN Radio Division produced it for broadcast on New Year’s Day 1949, when the Organization was still headquartered at Lake Success on Long Island. Copies would have been mailed to radio stations and UN offices around the world. Mr. Willens places it on a turntable with a microscope mounted above it, and the voices of actor Fredric March and sportscaster Ted Husing fill the room.Down the corridor, engineers are digitizing the archive of William Greaves, a pioneering African American documentary filmmaker. His 2001 film Ralph Bunche: An American Odyssey tells the story of the American diplomat who won the 1950 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating the armistice agreements between Israel and Arab States. Mr. Bunche was the first Black Nobel laureate and later became UN Under-Secretary-General.‘Kind of like surgery’Time is working against all of it. The acetate film which the New York Public Library is trying to preserve suffers from “vinegar syndrome,” a chemical decay that leaves it brittle, warped and smelling of vinegar. “Once that process starts, there’s no stopping it,” Ms. McNamara said. “You can slow it down with cold storage, but it will never reverse.” UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva Victoria Fajardo - Media Preservation Engineer, Audio. Audiotape can arrive crinkled or stuck together and must be repaired by hand. “To be able to repair it and then play it and get a successful transfer is kind of like surgery,” said media preservation engineer Victoria Fajardo. “It really is such a privilege to be one of the first people to listen to a lot of this content for the first time since it’s been recorded.”Even Digital Betacam cassettes, once considered robust, have started to shed. Francis Dougherty, the specialist who originally built the video lab, now has to clean his deck between tapes. “Every year this job gets more difficult,” he said. “Every year physical media degrades.”The last of the repairmen“The machines are getting rarer,” Mr. Dougherty added. “The old men who repair the machines are getting even rarer.” UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva Francis Dougherty originally built the lab for NYPL. Asked how urgent the work is, he does not hesitate: “It should have been dealt with 20 years ago.”Universities train young specialists but there are fewer and fewer machines for them to work on.“Without people to maintain and repair and service them, we won’t be able to do this,” Mr. Dowlatshahi added. “And there’s only a few people that do it now.”Work in progressSome solutions are built by hand. The turntable that played the UN disc was made by Nick Bergh, a California engineer who builds playback machines as “sort of a hobby.” The library has one of the first in the world.It isn’t even finished. For now, its microscope lets engineers inspect record grooves for scratches; eventually, a second arm will read discs optically, without touching them.Bergh’s earlier machine uses lasers to align warped wax cylinders to within microns and to read broken ones without contact. The library used it to re-transfer the Mapleson Cylinders, recorded at the Metropolitan Opera in the early 1900s. They hold “unique performances by singers who were never otherwise recorded.”The paradox according to Mr. Willens is that as playback technology improves, the original recordings keep deteriorating. Every year of waiting means less heritage left to save. ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: COP17: The world has a plan to save nature. Is it working?
content: COP17: The world has a plan to save nature. Is it working? 17 October 2026 Climate and Environment The UN Secretary-General has called for an end to the “war on nature”. On Monday, governments gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, will have to confront a more practical question: are they doing enough to win the peace and put the world’s biodiversity goals back on track? COP17, the UN Biodiversity Conference, comes at a critical halfway point in the global effort to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. Running from 19 to 30 October, the meeting will take stock of progress, identify where countries are falling behind and, crucially, consider how to accelerate action over the next four years. Here’s what you need to know:First things first: What is the global biodiversity framework?The big picture: Think of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as the world’s blueprint for halting and reversing the destruction of nature.Agreed in 2022, it contains 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals for 2050. It tackles the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species. Its best known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). But, the framework goes much further, including financing for biodiversity, reforming harmful incentives, encouraging more sustainable production and consumption and addressing businesses’ impacts and dependencies on nature. So, how are we doing?Reality check: We’re not moving fast enough.There has been movement. Nearly 90 per cent of the 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 per cent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans and more than 70 per cent have submitted national reports. But, fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties are on track. Ambition also remains short of the 30-by-30 goal, while major gaps persist in finance, capacity, cooperation and the data needed to track progress. As Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders in Yerevan on Friday: “Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability.”What’s actually on the table at COP17?Why it matters: COP17 is essentially about moving from promises to delivery.Among the big issues governments will grapple with:Taking stock: Countries will undertake the first global review of collective progress under the framework, examining what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed. Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Paruyr Hovhannisyan.Making the Cali Fund work: Governments will have an opportunity to advance practical arrangements for the fund, designed to support fair and equitable benefit-sharing from commercial use of digital sequence information on genetic resources.Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results. Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives. © Unsplash/Jack5parrow City skyline beneath snow-capped Mount Ararat, Armenia. Yerevan’s testFor host Armenia, success means COP17 becoming both a “review COP” and an “implementation COP”.“We cannot treat 2030 as a distant deadline,” Ambassador Hovhannisyan told UN News. “Decisions taken in Yerevan must help close the gap between commitments and results on the ground.”Hambardzum Matevosyan, Armenia’s Environment Minister and incoming COP17 president, puts the progression simply: COP15 produced the framework and COP16 advanced mechanisms to implement it. COP17, he said, must establish “where we stand, what is working, where progress is falling short and what must change”. The bottom lineBiodiversity can sound abstract. Its loss is anything but.As António Guterres reminded leaders on Friday, the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe depend on it. The question in Yerevan is whether countries can turn an ambitious global agreement into action quickly enough.On Thursday, launching a major UN report evaluating global progress under the landmark Kunming framework, Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, distilled the challenge: “We know where we stand. We know where the gaps are. Now, we must work together to close them.” ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. biodiversity2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

title: Flour sacks turned flood barriers: Gaza faces another winter without safe shelter
content: Flour sacks turned flood barriers: Gaza faces another winter without safe shelter 17 October 2026 Humanitarian Aid Like many people in the war-ravaged Gaza Strip, Ahmed Al-Omari is preparing for another winter of bitter cold and rain that threatens to cause flooding as families struggle to survive in tattered tents and damaged buildings. He is racing against time, working with other young men to fill sacks that once held World Food Programme (WFP) flour with sand to protect their makeshift shelters from the rain.“These are flour sacks that we used to retrieve from the jaws of death, so that we could eat,” he told UN News, referring to the dangers of aid distribution in the Gaza Strip, where civilians have been killed while trying to obtain assistance.“Now, they have become sacks that we fill with sand to act as barriers against rainwater,” he explained. “We flood every year and we have put these sacks in place in the hope that, somehow, rainwater will not get inside.”Two million need better shelterAround two million people in Gaza still need shelter assistance, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Rain has already begun and an intensifying El Niño threatens more in the coming months.Right now, agencies were working to get as much shelter material into the Strip as possible before winter, Karl Baker, IOM’s regional crisis coordinator for Gaza, said from Amman, Jordan.“We know that the rains have already begun and that the volume of goods that we have to get into Gaza is not going to meet the demands of the population,” he said.Funding shortages that began to decline in January have hampered preparations, Mr. Baker said.“The funding has come a little later in the year. It is now arriving, but it’s not at the scale needed to support what we estimate is 1.8 to 1.9 million people needing some sort of shelter assistance,” he said. UN News Tents sheltering displaced people crowd Unknown Soldier Square in Gaza City’s Rimal neighbourhood. Shipping routes disruptedThe continuing regional conflict is also disrupting supply chains. IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India and Pakistan, with goods routed through Jordan, Egypt and Israel before reaching Gaza.“The other point, of course, is that the regional conflict seems to be only growing. That disrupts trade routes,” Mr. Baker said.As long as the global shipping is disrupted, it will delay the volume or the timing for goods to reach Gaza, he added.Tents that last six monthsQuality is another concern. In other emergencies, Mr. Baker said, IOM could provide more durable transitional shelter, such as plywood and relief housing units.In Gaza, tents typically last only about six months. With people constantly displaced, they are often destroyed or left behind when families flee at short notice.“Constantly moving a tent or a temporary structure has caused, I would say, a lack of quality for what is currently inside of Gaza,” he said. “The quality needs to be enhanced with either more durable items or more goods, which currently help with temporary solutions.” UN News Residents continue to live in damaged residential buildings in Gaza despite the risk of collapse. An impossible choiceMore than 4,000 buildings, many of them home to thousands of residents, are reportedly at risk of collapse.Briefing the UN Security Council, Ramiz Alakbarov, acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, said the UN was working with local communities to evacuate people from unsafe buildings. With no alternatives, many had little choice but to seek shelter in tents.Recalling a recent visit to Gaza, he described the impossible decisions facing families: leave the homes they had returned to or stay in buildings at risk of collapse.Living space is also shrinking. Only around 30 per cent of Gaza is now accessible to most people, IOM’s Mr. Baker said.Conditions in displacement sites continue to deteriorate, humanitarian assessments show, with many exposed to flooding and few alternative places to go.‘New experiment’In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, families are salvaging materials from the rubble. Displaced from Rafah, Mohammed Barhoum and his sons are using metal rods recovered from the wreckage to try to strengthen their shelter.It is risky work amid unstable debris and explosive remnants of war.“Every year during the winter, this area floods because of heavy rainfall,” Mr. Barhoum said. “This year, we decided to reinforce our tents using metal rods. It is a new experiment, and we will see how it goes. We hope the situation will be better than it was last time.” UN News Palestinians are building stronger tents using iron rods salvaged from rubble and plastic sheeting in preparation for winter. Durable materials blockedMost of the durable shelter materials IOM would normally use in emergencies fall under Israel’s dual-use restrictions, which date back to 2008. They include roofing sheets, cement for floors and stronger walls to withstand the wind – items that could make shelters more resistant to winter, but are often deemed a security concern.Mr. Baker said IOM was in repeated contact with the Israeli authorities to negotiate their entry.“It is an everyday occurrence, five times per day, as we try to negotiate or we try to make sure that we have actually either understood what their concern is and trying to adjust whatever that might be,” he said.“From our perspective, we must continue to advocate for more durable items to get in.” Soundcloud ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: As disasters mount, next UN climate summit faces a test of trust
content: As disasters mount, next UN climate summit faces a test of trust By Laura Quinones 16 October 2026 Climate and Environment Less than a month before the UN climate conference COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, representatives of three successive summit presidencies gathered to address a pressing question: How can the world restore trust in climate action when the consequences of a warming planet are already being felt? The devastation in Nepal offered a stark reminder of what is at stake. Opening the high-level meeting at UN Headquarters, General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman evoked the imagery of a wall of water barreling down a mountain valley, sweeping away people, homes and communities in its path.“Scientists had long warned that such events were becoming a reality, yet none of us were prepared for the shocking footage”.He reminded delegates that this year's strengthening El Niño could be among the strongest since at least 1950, while the world is on its way to hotting up by 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels under current climate policies, far beyond the Paris Agreement's goals.“Behind these figures are families uprooted, children's missing, school women walking farther for water, and communities confronting losses they cannot bear,” the assembly president added.The task ahead for world leaders at the upcoming climate conference COP31 is to then turn commitments into action – and promises into trust, he said. “COP31 must be more than another negotiating milestone. It must demonstrate that multilateralism delivers.”From promises, to investmentTürkiye, which will host the conference from 9 to 20 November, outlined plans to accelerate clean energy, reduce methane emissions and strengthen climate resilience.Among the key initiatives for this COP is the Climate Implementation Bridge, developed with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), which aims to transform national climate commitments into investment-ready projects and connect them with financing.“The issue is not simply the overall volume of finance. It is also whether finance is available, accessible, affordable and predictable,” Türkiye's Ambassador to the UN, Ahmet Yıldız said.For Pacific island nations, the need for action is already immediate. Rising seas and extreme weather are threatening homes, livelihoods and infrastructure, a reality highlighted by Australia, which is leading the COP31 negotiations under an unprecedented arrangement that sees two countries thousands of miles apart, sharing responsibilities for the climate summit.“By listening to our most vulnerable communities, partnering with those in need, and accelerating the implementation of practical initiatives, I believe we can restore trust through climate action,” Australian Ambassador James Larsen said.Mr Larsen called for more accessible climate financing and stronger adaptation plans grounded in science and local needs.Difficult negotiations aheadBrazil, which hosted COP30 last year, identified three priorities for Antalya: Making the new just transition mechanism operational, improving how countries measure progress on adaptation expanding climate investment in developing countries struggling with debt“In a world of States with severe fiscal constraints and high indebtedness, the [finance] talks need to lead to viable solutions for expanding fiscal space for climate investment,” Ambassador Sérgio França Danese urged.The question of who pays, and who benefits, also runs through Ethiopia’s concerns, which will host COP32.Africa contributes only around three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, Ambassador Tesfaye Yilma Sabo reminded delegates, yet faces some of the most severe consequences of climate change.“Delayed action carries a compounding cost for developing countries. The pace of action matters because the gap between current plans and what the science requires remains significant.Financing and access to technology are increasingly determining who benefits from the transition and who is left behind,” he warned.World leaders are expected to gather for a special summit in Antalya on 11 and 12 November, with negotiations set to test whether climate commitments can translate into meaningful change for communities most at risk.But for Mr. Rahman, the measure of success will be found far beyond the negotiating rooms.“Let COP31 be judged not by promises we repeat, but by the people we protect. That is how we restore trust.” ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices.

title: Ukraine: Civilian casualty rates among ‘deadliest’ in years, as energy attacks intensify
content: Ukraine: Civilian casualty rates among ‘deadliest’ in years, as energy attacks intensify 16 October 2026 Peace and Security Civilian casualties in Ukraine remain at record levels, with intensified Russian attacks in September continuing a pattern of harm in 2026 far exceeding previous years, UN human rights monitors in Ukraine said on Friday. The mission verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September – 85 per cent more than in September 2025. Casualties were recorded across 22 regions and the city of Kyiv, where civilians were killed or injured on 22 of the month’s 30 days, more often than in any month since the start of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion. Tweet URL The trend continued into October. On the night of 6 to 7 October alone, a Russian cruise missile and drone attack killed 22 civilians and injured 45 in Pryluky, in Chernihiv region.“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the human rights monitoring mission.Energy assaultThe high casualties came as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure. On 13 and 14 October, strikes hit multiple energy facilities, including Kyiv’s three main power stations, temporarily leaving 600,000 people in the capital without electricity, according to Ukrainian authorities.Ukrainian armed forces also targeted electricity and heating infrastructure in occupied territory and in the Russian Federation, the mission said.“Systematically attacking electricity and heating infrastructure as winter approaches is bound to inflict significant suffering on the civilian population,” Ms. Bell warned.Risk of displacementDamaged homes and attacks on energy also risk forcing Ukrainians who have returned home to flee again this winter, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) warned.“For millions of Ukrainians, the challenge is no longer simply whether they can return home. It is whether they can remain there safely and right now the conditions are making it difficult,” said Arthur Erken, IOM Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia.Some 1.45 million returnees now live in frontline districts, and during the last cold season only 32 per cent of households could heat their homes adequately. Around 2.1 million older people live alone in apartment buildings, leaving them especially exposed to prolonged power and heating cuts.Less than seven per cent of IOM’s crisis response plan for Ukraine this year has been funded, Mr. Erken said, calling for urgent support to repair homes, improve insulation and maintain essential services.Another diesel shortageMeanwhile, the eighth localised ceasefire brokered by the international nuclear energy watchdog (IAEA) between Ukraine and Russia, began on Thursday to allow repairs to a damaged backup transformer, strengthening the connection between the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant and its sole remaining external power line.IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi welcomed the cooperation of both sides but warned that diesel fuel at the plant was running low, with no deliveries since March.“It is essential that steps are taken to increase the volume of diesel fuel available on-site prior to winter, when the situation may become acute,” he said, renewing his call for maximum military restraint from all sides. ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents
content: WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents 16 October 2026 Health The World Health Organization (WHO) is strengthening Ebola preparedness amid conflict and displacement affecting millions of lives in a region that spans parts of Africa, Asia and Europe. The UN agency’s eastern Mediterranean region comprises 22 countries and territories. Intensified support is being given to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, which have been identified as priority countries.This follows deadly outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in both the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda and confirmation of a case in Kenya linked to the DRC. Soundcloud Hostilities and overstretched health systemsAlthough there have not been any Ebola cases in the region so far, conflict, displacement and overstretched health systems in several countries are making it difficult to prepare and respond should the situation change.In a speech earlier this week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Gebreyesus described the region as “the epicentre of global humanitarian need”. More than 117 million people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Sudan, Syria, Yemen and beyond, require humanitarian assistance to survive.Assessing readiness, identifying challengesBetween July and September, WHO deployed missions to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan to assess national readiness and identify challenges in Ebola surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination. The UN agency is helping authorities to address gaps through training, technical support, medical supplies and simulation exercises.It has developed regional readiness checklists, contingency planning tools and technical guidance, in addition to strengthening coordination with countries in both Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. WHO has also provided laboratory supplies, traveller guidance and community engagement resources.Despite progress, gaps remain in early detection, laboratory confirmation and availability of protective equipment and resources for emergency response. “Conflict, insecurity and restricted access present additional challenges, particularly in countries already facing major humanitarian emergencies,” WHO said.Meanwhile, work continues to ensure that national authorities and partners can rapidly detect, investigate and manage suspected Ebola cases. ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: Gaza: 340 children killed despite ceasefire agreement - UNICEF
content: Gaza: 340 children killed despite ceasefire agreement - UNICEF By Daniel Johnson in Geneva 16 October 2026 Peace and Security A little over one year since a ceasefire agreement was announced between Hamas fighters and Israel, more than 340 children have been reported killed and hundreds more injured, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday. For families “mourning the loss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire”, stressed spokesperson Ricardo Pires.He added that in the last two weeks in Gaza alone, five boys and two girls have been reported killed and at least 33 children seriously injured in airstrikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the Strip. Another two boys died of injuries sustained previously, Mr. Pires told journalists in Geneva.Nowhere is safeThe consequences of the Hamas-Israel war are everywhere for children: “where they sleep, what they eat, whether they can learn”, he continued, citing the case of Tweet URL 16-year-old Norhan whose mother was shot while eight months pregnant. “She delivered her baby and then died the following day,” Mr. Pires explained. “Norhan’s father is living with a disability, so she now cares for her one-year-old sister Narjis and takes full responsibility. Her days are spent tidying the home, cooking, and playing with Narjis. Her three other siblings attend a UNICEF-supported learning centre and Norhan helps them with their studies after class, which as she says means, ‘They might just have a future.’”Asked about reports that private traders in Gaza had halted cooperation with the Israeli authorities on allowing commercial trucks carrying food to enter the occupied enclave, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed that the uninterrupted flow of “humanitarian and commercial goods” remained essential, “so children can continue their recovery”.He recalled being in Gaza City last year before the ceasefire began, when supplies “were not getting in” and famine was declared by UN-backed food insecurity experts. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he insisted, “where children are not receiving what they need to survive and to continue to have hope for their future”.Winter alertThe UNICEF alert comes as temperatures drop and displaced families in Gaza fill empty flour bags with sand to keep rainwater out of their tents. Aid agencies continue to repeat warnings that the situation in Gaza remains dire, after three years of war, sparked by Hamas-led terror attacks in Israel.The ongoing sanitation crisis is a particular concern in the war-torn enclave, where Israeli bombardment has severely damaged the drainage network.“There are vast pools of wastewater, such as the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin that is half-full,” Mr. Pires warned. “With the winter rains fast approaching, we’re running out of time to pump this out. Just as we warned a year ago, contaminated water could overflow and inundate downstream residential areas with potentially life-threatening impacts for children and their families. Children have drowned in sewage-contaminated water before.”No shelterAccording to UNICEF, 800,000 children remain displaced in Gaza “and most live in tents or dangerous bombed-out buildings”. An estimated 60,000 children have seen either one or both parents killed during the war, or since the ceasefire, while nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover.As part of UN assistance to Palestinians in Gaza, UNICEF has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including at over 200 UNICEF-supported learning centres. The agency has also provided digital cash assistance – “a lifeline”, Mr. Pires stressed – to more than 380,000 people, along with safe water to 1.2 million people. ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. title: Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
content: The United Nations Secretary-General appealed on Friday for governments, businesses and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations and all life on Earth.

title: Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology
content: Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to protect human rights.

title: The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
content: Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.

title: AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns
content: Rapid transformations – from artificial intelligence and digital technologies to renewable energy and demographic shifts – are reshaping economies worldwide, creating new opportunities but also threatening to deepen socio-economic inequalities, a new UN report warned on Thursday.

title: Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations
content: Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global hunger monitor report released on Thursday.

title: Ukraine: Critical health supplies destroyed in ongoing Russian attacks
content: Ongoing and deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine are causing serious healthcare disruption, with more than $1.5 million-worth of medicines and supplies destroyed in four separate strikes on warehouses used by the UN there since July.

title: WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to support Kenya’s efforts to contain Ebola after a second person tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus, the UN agency’s representative in the country said on Thursday.

title: Security Council LIVE: Deaths, demolitions spike in Gaza, West Bank
content: Amid a rise in lethal Israeli strikes, demolitions and violence in Gaza and the West Bank, the Security Council held an open debate on Thursday focusing on the current situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

title: WHO urges faster action to end lead exposure which kills 3.5 million annually
content: Countries must accelerate efforts to prevent lead exposure, which is estimated to cause more than 3.5 million deaths globally each year and affects hundreds of millions of children, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Thursday.

title: Haiti sanctions renewed: Starving the gangs of bullets
content:
Haiti is living through one of the world’s most acute security crises.
Armed gangs control large parts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and are pushing into rural areas, terrorising communities, killing people, committing rape and other sexual assaults, kidnapping for ransom and extorting individuals and businesses.

title: Colombia: UN independent experts call for Ecopetrol to provide reparations to victims of armed conflict
content: UN independent experts welcomed on Wednesday a recent landmark corporate accountability ruling involving the Ecopetrol oil company by Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, calling for reparations for victims.

title: World News in Brief: Gaza braces for winter amid attacks, joint patrols in CAR, 90 cities commit to sustainable development
content: The UN and its partners are stepping up preparations in Gaza for the approaching cold and rainy season, even as attacks affecting civilians continue, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said on Wednesday.

title: DR Congo: Cholera cases spike amid fight against Ebola
content: The cholera epidemic continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 125,000 suspected cases and 3,644 suspected deaths were recorded between January 2025 and the end of September 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned on Wednesday.

title: Health workers tackle taboos over drinking with new AI tool
content: A new AI-powered hub for health professionals aims to help identify alcohol-related risks and launch discussions with patients, including the link between drinking and cancer, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced on Wednesday.

title: Security Council LIVE: Libya in the spotlight amid ‘encouraging progress’
content: Despite progress in the political process in Libya, institutional divisions, economic deterioration and security fragility continue to threaten stability, the UN envoy warned the Security Council on Wednesday, calling on Libyan leaders to overcome their differences to pave the way for national elections.

title: Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
content: Intensifying fighting in Yemen has cut off life-saving assistance to 800,000 people as shifting frontlines, blocked roads and growing insecurity severely restrict access to the city of Taiz and other conflict zones, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said on Wednesday.

title: WHO calls for urgent health action across the Eastern Mediterranean
content: The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world’s top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

title: Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs
content: Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.

title: 800 million young people face a future without jobs
content: Approximately 800 million young people entering the labour market in developing economies over the coming years will not find jobs unless countries act, the head of the UN Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Tuesday, as the agency launched two initiatives to boost investment and employment.

title: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
content: Fewer people from West Africa are reaching Europe by sea, but the journey has not become safer, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Tuesday.

title: ‘Need for UN has never been greater,’ UN chief says, proposing slimmer $3.3 billion budget for 2027
content: Amid climate disruption, an AI revolution, war and growing hunger, “the need for the United Nations has never been greater,” Secretary-General António Guterres said on Tuesday, presenting a $3.3 billion programme budget proposal for next year – a cut of $40.8 million.

title: Drone attack near southern Sudan market kills scores
content: Advertising Drone attack near southern Sudan market kills scores Africa At least 80 people were killed in a drone strike near a market in Sudan’s southern West Kordofan state, a medical source and a witness said Monday. The strike in the town of Al-Dibab on Sunday evening is among the deadliest single attacks since war erupted between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in 2023. Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 16:00 1 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 File photo: Members of the pro-Sudanese army popular resistance group gather for a rally supporting the army position in Darfur, Kordofan, and the Blue Nile State, in the Karary district of Omdurman, the twin-city of Sudan's capital, on June 30, 2026. © Ebrahim Hamid, AFP A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching trucks home, a medical source and a witness told AFP on Monday. The strike in the town of Al-Dibab in West Kordofan state on Sunday evening left "50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed", Ahmed Abakar Wadi told AFP, using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout. He said 47 others were transported to the nearest town, Al-Mujlad, where 30 of them died from injuries, a medical source told AFP. Read moreUN warns drone attacks have become leading cause of civilian death in Sudan "A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on Al-Dibab, and another drone strike on Al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated," the medic said, requesting anonymity for his safety. The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Read moreAt least 82 killed in gold mine collapse in remote area of Sudan, paramilitary RSF say The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out the strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control. Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, "on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends". There is no definite toll from the conflict as a whole, but aid workers estimate it has killed more than 200,000 people, besides creating the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis.
