title: 'Shame', 'anger', 'chaos': Papers react to polarising riots in France
content: 'Shame', 'anger', 'chaos': Papers react to polarising riots in France France To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement. Accept Manage my choices One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site. Try again Cover image: PRESS REVIEW © FRANCE 24 05:53 Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 12:11Modified: 19/10/2026 - 12:12 05:53 min Share From the show Reading time 3 min PRESS REVIEW – Monday, October 19: French and international papers discuss the anti-government protests that turned violent at the weekend and their aftermath across France. Many French papers are using the word "chaos" to describe the protests over the weekend. Le Parisien writes: "After the chaos, the anger". It says that on Sunday France woke up to destruction following the protests. The headline of left-wing paper Libération reads "Questioning chaos". Libération says that due to an inadequate law enforcement strategy that failed to anticipate the widespread vandalism and looting, the protests spiralled out of control, although hundreds of thousands of people were attempting to march peacefully. The headline of right-wing paper Le Figaro reads "Shame and anger". The paper says that all across France "unprecedented scenes of violence" took place, which are causing consternation. The headline of the Communist paper L'Humanité reads "Social explosion". The paper says that the day of protests was ruined by violence and vandalism, as well as by widespread police crackdowns on demonstrators. Catholic paper La Croix asks "How did we get here?" It says that the riots and looting are fuelling fears of widespread unrest, against a backdrop of social anger. L'Opinion asks: "Who benefits from the chaos?" The paper tries to summarise what happened: Public order has broken down. The prime minister is responding solely on a political level. The president is calling for calm. Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to stir up conflict, while far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is seeking to capitalise on both fronts: public order and social issues. International papers are also reacting. German newspaper Der Spiegel asks "Is France descending into chaos and crisis?" Politically, this unrest is going to further polarise France, according to the paper. One woman is likely to benefit, it says: the far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen. Le Pen and her National Rally party are skilfully presenting themselves as the guarantors of public order. This time, the right wing has refrained from actively supporting the movement, as it did in 2018 with the Yellow Vests, even though it expresses sympathy for the peaceful demonstrators; after all, many of their voters are among them. The headline of Spanish paper El País says "France sets Macronism ablaze". The paper calls President Emmanuel Macron's second term "out of touch with society" – but there are still six long months to go until the next presidential elections, during which the country must pass a budget and find answers to the unstoppable rise of the far right. The New York Times says there's "shock and recrimination", a day after the "huge riots". The paper says that during his speech, Macron "offered no concrete concessions". It reminds us that government officials and far-right leaders accuse the far left of stirring up the unrest. The left wing, meanwhile, blames the government for budget decisions and policies they said have spurred public anger. British paper The Times says that Paris was "divided by protests". Many are pointing the fingers at those who rioted and looted, saying the level of violence was worse than during the Yellow Vest protests in 2018. Others say that police repression pushed people to become increasingly violent. A 20-year-old art student told The Times: "Instead of listening to us, the government sends in the police to attack us". "We no longer live in a democracy" is the headline in the independent Russian paper Novaya Gazeta. It's a quote from one of the protesters who spoke to the paper. She says that "the Republic has been shaken to its core – we no longer live in a democracy where we can assemble," adding that "the police are seizing power through violence". You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday. title: French interior minister admits police 'lost control' of protests
content: France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted Monday that the police "lost control" in some cities during violent protests that erupted in cities across the country at the weekend. He said there had been a "lack of anticipation" in preparations and that he had tendered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron "because I felt responsible for everything that happened." Macron did not accept his resignation.

title: World Food Programme to end aid for half a million in Gaza due to funding shortfall
content: Advertising World Food Programme to end aid for half a million in Gaza due to funding shortfall Middle East The UN World Food Programme has warned that funding shortages will leave about 500,000 people in the Gaza Strip without critical food aid in a territory where two thirds of the population remains acutely food insecure. The WFP said it is reducing its monthly assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people. Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 09:33 1 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 Palestinians line up to receive food donated by the World Food Programme at a displacement camp in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, on October 18, 2026. © Abdel Kareem Hana, AP The UN's World Food Programme (WFP) said on Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, while warning that needs remained acute. "As of this month, we're now cutting half a million people from the number of people that we're assisting," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP. The reductions bring down the number of Palestinians receiving WFP aid either in food or cash assistance to 1.1 million people – still roughly half of war-battered Gaza's population. title: 'Quite horrifying': Afghan economic crisis leaves EU deportees with 'very little' to return to
content: Europe's increasingly pragmatic engagement with Afghanistan's Taliban rulers is exposing a fundamental contradiction between diplomatic non-recognition and political necessity. In an investigation for The New York Times, Pakistan and Afghanistan bureau chief Elian Peltier reveals how European governments are quietly expanding negotiations with the Taliban over migrant deportations, diplomatic representation and economic assistance. “Even though on paper European governments do not recognise the Taliban administration, in practice they meet much more frequently than most of us know,” Peltier explains.

title: Russia pounds Kyiv as Rubio urges Ukraine's Zelensky to 'focus' on ending the war
content: Advertising Russia pounds Kyiv as Rubio urges Ukraine's Zelensky to 'focus' on ending the war Europe Russia on Monday said it carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and its region as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington had paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine and urged its president Volodymyr Zelensky to focus on ending the war. Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 08:00Modified: 19/10/2026 - 08:35 1 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 Police officers inspect a building hit by a Russian missile strike in Kyiv on October 19, 2026. © Valentyn Ogirenko, Reuters The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and the Ukraine's capital region. The ministry said the attack targeted military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones, and data centres. The latest attacks came as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that there had been any suspension of intelligence sharing with Ukraine and called on President Volodymyr Zelensky to "focus" on ending the war with Russia. "What he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," Rubio said while on a trip to Uzbekistan for talks with Central Asian leaders. He said there had been no "pause" in the sharing of intelligence as Kyiv authorities have claimed. Read moreWhy have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms? US President Donald Trump, who made a deal with Russia to secure fuel exports in exchange for the easing of sanctions, has made renewed attacks on Zelensky in recent days over the war. The US leader wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that he was making "great progress" in negotiating peace between Russia and Ukraine, but claimed: "Zelensky doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." "Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said. (FRANCE 24 with AFP, Reuters) Advertising Keywords for this article Ukraine Russia Kyiv Marco Rubio

title: ‘Not a problem of short-term solutions’: French students demand structural change, better conditions
content: Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Gökçe Tuncel, Sociologist and post-doctoral researcher associated with the Université Paris-Est Créteil (UPEC) and the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (EHESS) in Paris. What began as a protest over missing teachers and inadequate resources at a high school in Créteil has rapidly evolved into a wider mobilization challenging structural inequalities within France’s public education system. “This is not a problem of short-term solutions. This is a structural problem that they are denouncing, and their demands are structural changes,” explains Tuncel. The movement's rapid expansion reflects a growing political consciousness among young people confronting deteriorating educational infrastructure, unequal access to resources, and an increasingly uncertain future.

title: 'We don't have to wait for others to support us': Myanmar refugees find hope in Thailand's work program
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OP4LThailand's work program has allowed thousands of Myanmar refugees living in camps to support themselves and their families [FILE: May 28, 2024]Image: Matt Hunt/NurPhoto/picture allianceAdvertisementAt a glance, Ray Boe doesn't stand out from the tens of thousands of other foreign workers toiling at countless construction sites that push Bangkok's soaring skyline ever higher. Unlike most of them, though, the 31-year-old came to Thailand's capital from one of the country's nine camps for refugees who have fled Myanmar's decades of civil strife. The camps, which hug the Thai-Myanmar border, are home to more than 100,000 people — in some cases since the 1980s when the refugees first started arriving. Until a year ago this month, the Thai government had refused to let them leave the camps to find work, forcing most to live hand-to-mouth on foreign donor aid. That changed in October 2025, after foreign aid cutbacks — mostly by the United States — forced the camps to slash the food support and healthcare they could provide. Around the same time, fighting between Thailand and Cambodia over territorial claims had sent hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from Cambodia back home, leaving behind a yawning labor gap. New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugeesTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Myanmar refugees allowed to work outside of camps To cope with the aid cuts and labor deficit, the Thai government reversed decades of policy and began issuing the refugees permits to work outside the camps, to help them meet their own needs. Ray Boe is one of the 6,800 camp refugees the government says have entered the Thai labor force in the first year of the program. "After the cuts by USAID and other organizations, there is no more regular support for our daily needs, like rice and other rations. And there is not enough healthcare in the camps anymore," he said. The cuts forced him and his parents to borrow from neighbors and to pare down their already modest meals. Since last month, he has earned 400 baht (about $12) a day pouring concrete and erecting scaffolding around what's to be a 12-story apartment building in central Bangkok. He hopes to start sending money home soon. "It will help us pay for food and other basic needs, and for health care for my parents," Ray Boe said. "Compared to how we were living in the camp before, it will be a big difference, having my own income and supporting my family on my own, not having to wait for other people to support us day to day," he told DW. Underpaid and overworked: Myanmar migrants in ThailandTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Refugee work program offers hope but faces a rocky start The program allows the refugees to work in 43 of Thailand's 76 provinces and in any sector not reserved by law for Thai citizens only. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the government has improved the vocational training on offer inside the camps to better prepare refugees for work outside. "We are hopeful that this policy would enhance opportunities and empower the [refugees] to realize their potential, as well as contribute to Thai socio-economic development," said Praporn Waenluang, a spokesman for the ministry's information department. Labor and refugee rights groups have welcomed the program. "I have met a lot of camp [refugees] who have come outside and worked. They are so happy to work and earn money, a lot of money compared to what they [can] get in the camp," said Siwawong Sooktawee, Thailand project coordinator for the International Detention Coalition. "This is good because they feel they can help themselves, they can support themselves, not depend on aid anymore," he added. Yet he and others say the program has gotten off to a slow start, with many flaws to work out. They say many of the refugees who have taken part have not been given contracts by their employers, only to find the conditions rougher, the work harder, or the pay lower than what they were promised before leaving the camps. The program also lacks a clear system for lodging and settling complaints, they say. "Many refugees go, come back, go, come back so many times. Some refugees, their families have to raise funds or borrow money in the refugee camps so that their father or their family member will be able to return," said K'nyaw Paw, general secretary of the Karen Women's Organization, an NGO serving the camp's ethnic Karen. Myanmar workers in Thailand struggle to work legallyTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Financial burdens placed on Myanmar refugees Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw say refugees are sometimes made to repay employers through wage deductions for hiring them, including medical exams, government permits and transportation to job sites. As a result, they often start work already in debt, sometimes without prior warning. Akwah, a father of two who goes by one name, left his camp with 20 other refugees in November 2025 for what was supposed to be a job harvesting sugarcane on a farm on the other side of the country for 250 baht per day. When he arrived, however, he was told to cut eucalyptus trees — a much more difficult and dangerous job, he says — for 200 baht per day. They had to sleep outdoors, with no electricity and only a nearby pond for water. "We spoke to the boss, but the boss did not care. He said, 'Just do the work because you are already here.' But we said we could not do it," said Akwah, and they left after three months. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply to DW's request for comment on the program's alleged problems. The Labor and Interior Ministries, which mainly oversee the program, did not reply to requests for an interview either. Rights groups say program still needs to improve Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw say refugees who take part should be guaranteed clear and detailed contracts — translated if needed into Burmese, Karen or Karenni, the main languages spoken in the camps — and an easy-to-access system for filing and settling complaints. They also suggest that the government open more provinces up to the program and screen the job brokers coming to the camps as middlemen, to weed out the unscrupulous ones. They say their NGOs and others are working with the government on making some of the upgrades, and that they're hopeful the program will improve with time, so that more of the refugees are able and willing to take part. For all the program's flaws, though, they say most of the refugees are still eager to apply, even those who have run into problems. "I had a bad experience, but I still want to go again, because food in the camp is a problem," said Mu Dah Hsit, who fell ill at her job and had to quit after her boss refused to cover the health insurance the program is supposed to guarantee. "I have no mother, and a father who is sick, and siblings I have to take care of," she said. "So, I have to go; otherwise, we cannot live." title: Marco Rubio visits India this week, with a trip to the world's largest oil refinery topping the agenda
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OPZ4Ahead of his arrival in India, Rubio said a trade deal was 'close' Image: Kylie Cooper/REUTERSAdvertisementUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries. Rubio's business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India's purchases of Russian oil. Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it's a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India's energy relationship with Russia. In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance. US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched. An elusive US-India trade deal Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India's continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine. How India has become Russia's trade lifelineTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In February 2026, Trump announced a "trade deal" that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi. While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India's deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India's top supplier of crude oil. In mid-September, Trump signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act," imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India. However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions. Rubio: Trade deal 'very close' Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the "C5+1" diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind. Jamnagar is the largest single-site oil refinery in the worldImage: Reliance Industries Limited/AP Photo/picture alliance "We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said. "We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio added. In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US. Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. He said Jamnagar is an "important node in global trade" because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets. Although Trump's sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations. Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio's decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India. "The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar," she told DW. "The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue." Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices. Shankar pointed to Reliance's proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is "one of the states in play" in the upcoming midterm elections in the US. "Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome," she said. Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Trump eroding trust in Delhi? The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy. Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading. "Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values," he said. The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing. Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers. On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers. The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals. Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump's own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement. "Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians," Pant told DW. Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump's presidency. "The sense that America is unreliable, that America can't be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse," he said. The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements. "If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals "will have consequences." title: Half a million Palestinians in Gaza are to lose food support amid WFP funding shortage
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OPSKThe cut to aid comes with winter approaching and no end in sight for the conflictImage: Jehad Alshrafi/AP Photo/dpa/picture allianceAdvertisementThe United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has been forced to cut its monthly food aid to the war-ravaged Gaza Strip , where some two-thirds of the population are struggling to get food, the agency said on Monday. The WFP said it was reducing the number of people receiving aid from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving some 500,000 people without support. The UN program is facing severe funding shortages. "WFP no longer has sufficient funding to sustain this level of support," the organization said. What UN aid is being cut in Gaza? Beyond the cutting of aid to some half a million recipients in the region, the WFP is also: Reducing rations by half Cash assistance has been cut for some 75,000 families Hot meals for those unable to cook have been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000 Some 1.4 million people in Gaza are facing crisis levels of food insecurity according to the WFP, with 200,000 living in emergency conditions. Despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect last year, Israeli strikes have continued and aid has remained restricted, with little progress toward a final end to the conflict. "It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no ⁠basic ​services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive ​Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza. "These cuts are happening ​just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added. Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into warTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why is aid being cut to Gaza? The UN program urgently needs $450 million (€400 million) to keep funding its critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months. "We tell the world now ⁠is not ​the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," Skau said. The WFP had already announced cuts to aid for the West Bank in early September, citing funding shortages and donor fatigue. The Israeli authority responsible for the Palestinian territories, COGAT, says the supply of aid deliveries into the strip exceeds the demand for food and it claims there is no acute food insecurity in Gaza. title: The Rainfall Market: Korean writer You Yeong-Gwang's journey from delivery driver to bestselling author
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OIWTThe book was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and ChineseImage: ClayHouse/Michael Joseph/AceAdvertisementFor ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights. "I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair. For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese. "The Rainfall Market" tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space. "In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness." While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself. "I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected. "But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it." On the creation of 'The Rainfall Market' The idea of rain is inspired by his own life. "At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.You Yeong-gwang, author of 'The Rainfall Market'Image: ClayHouse The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives. "When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed." He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.” "At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years." He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own. While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery driver. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway." "Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained. Finally a breakthrough "I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said. The campaign was intended to fund the publication of "The Rainfall Market." "To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.How K-pop pushes appetite for Korean ramyun noodlesTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company. Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts. And in the first month after publication, the original South Korean language edition sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book. "I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You. A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave:' K-Comfort Fiction Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year. And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction. "When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said. Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market and intense corporate pressure. "When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered. With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair. The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.How South Korea is cashing in on 'KPop Demon Hunters'To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world. Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was "Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop," according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. The novel belongs to the same genre as "The Rainfall Market." While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development. Reviewing "The Rainfall Market" for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets. Future aspirations and message to readers "Of course I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," You said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair. Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life. "If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru Advertisement

title: This homeless man has lived in front of one of London's most expensive houses for years. How?
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5N9o5Anders Fernstedt has built a home outside one of London's most expensive propertiesImage: Dan Redding/DWAdvertisementThere's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves. While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance. The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already. That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house. The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month. Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo. Chinese court hands Evergrande property tycoon life sentenceTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW. 'Camping on the balcony' Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding. "I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said. "My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."2-8A Rutland Gate sold for €244 million in 2020 but has been unoccupied sinceImage: Dan Redding/DW Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world. In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic. A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions. "Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said. Community support powers unusual lifestyle Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods. Fernstedt's home evolved over several years, through donations and giftsImage: Dan Redding/DW"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode. "It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears." There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming. "Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions." Homelessness a growing concern in London Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago." According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas." Britain's new PM takes on fight against homelessnessTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment. But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next. "I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy." Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier Advertisement

title: Greece: At least 12 people die in migrant boat accidents overnight in the eastern Mediterranean
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OOxcThousands of migrants have drowned in Greek waters trying to reach Europe over the past 11 years [FILE]Image: Sofianos Drapaniotis/REUTERSAdvertisementGreek Coast Guard officials say 12 migrants were killed in the Aegean Sea overnight in two separate boating accidents. In the first incident, six people — four men, a woman and an infant — were killed in waters off the coast of Lesbos when "a speedboat carrying migrants collided with the port side of a police patrol vessel," according to the Coast Guard. Eight people were reported rescued. In the second incident, six people — five men and a woman — drowned after their boat capsized off the coast of Samos, while 14 were rescued. A search-and-rescue mission is ongoing in the area. Authorities say they arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national among the survivors in the first incident, identifying him ‌as ​a suspected smuggler and the operator of the speedboat. Greece's Minister of Shipping and Island Policy Vassilis Kikilias blamed migrant traffickers for all of the deaths, posting on X, "Our position is non-negotiable: Zero tolerance for smugglers." Turkey to Greece: Deadly migrant passage to Europe Greece has long been a gateway ​to Europe for migrants and ⁠refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia who usually set off on the notoriously deadly sea voyage from Turkey. According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), refugee arrivals in Greece are declining this year. As of October 11, 2026, some 25,000 arrivals had been recorded compared to 42,000 in 2025. Almost one million migrants and refugees landed on Greece's shores during the 2015/2016 migration crisis, here, too, mainly from Turkey. title: Australian MP seriously hurt in suspected car attack
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OP08Helen Haines was elected to the Australian parliament in 2019Image: Mick Tsikas/AAP Image/AP Photo/picture allianceAdvertisementAustralian police are investigating a suspected car attack that has left independent MP Helen Haines with critical injuries. Counterterrorism investigators have joined the probe following the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne. What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines? Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, said by police to be a white Toyota, outside her office, leaving her with serious injuries, particularly to her lower body. Broadcaster ABC cited witnesses as saying they had heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Investigators are reported to have found a knife in the car.Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident'Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance Apparently deliberate attack: PM Albanese "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," Albanese told ABC. He said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence. "The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media." Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents." At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery." Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years. Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action. title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy says partners gave 'no warning' ahead of Russian ballistic strikes
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OOxAThe strikes hit Kyiv, including this candy shop in the city centerImage: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture allianceAdvertisementA barrage of Russian ballistic miles struck Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, killing at least one person and knocking out power to over half a million homes, Ukrainian authorities said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles, targeting Ukraine's energy facilities, 10 of which were hit, cutting power to some 550,000 households. The president also lamented the lack of warning from Ukraine's international partners. "Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," he wrote. Ukraine's Air Force reported strikes, which included cruise missiles and drones, hitting 25 locations. Of the 269 recorded Shahed drones deployed in the overnight attack, Ukrainian air defenses reportedly downed or suppressed 243, as well as four missiles.Ukraine strikes Putin's hometown, as Trump eases pressure on RussiaTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Moscow says it hit drone, missile hubs in Ukraine Russia's Defense Ministry also confirmed the "massive strikes" on Monday, saying it had targeted Ukraine with "ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones." The ministry said it had hit a Ukrainian data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, a train depot storing missiles and an industrial facility involved in the production of drones. It also said it had struck a bulk carrier in the Black Sea, some 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the port of Odesa, which the ministry said had been carrying military and dual-use cargo. Ukraine did not confirm those targets but said that a medical facility had been hit in the capital, as well as one of the city's metro stations, according to a post by the Kyiv City Military Administration on Telegram.A police officer inspects the site of a fitness club that was hit by a missile Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Kyiv, Washington disagree over pause to intelligence sharing The overnight strikes come amid contradictory claims by both Ukraine and the US about pauses to intelligence sharing. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington had not paused some of its intelligence sharing, denying a statement Zelenskyy made on Sunday. "I don't know where [Zelenskyy's] getting these things ​or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause," Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan. "What he should ​focus on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That's what he should be focused on," he added. Ukraine is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. Some recent attacks have taken place without warning, Ukrainian officials have reported. title: West Bank: Israel arrests 10 suspects over settler attacks on US journalist, European diplomats
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OOheThe attack on veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine comes after global outrage over mounting settler violence in the West BankImage: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture allianceAdvertisementIsraeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 suspects over settler violence in the occupied West Bank, including attacks on a US photojournalist and European diplomats. Masked settlers were filmed assaulting The Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine on Friday while she was covering a Palestinian olive harvest, leaving her with broken vertebrae. The following day, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was visiting the West Bank to help with the harvest. The incidents drew condemnation from the United States, France, Belgium and Poland. Israeli police said the investigation was ongoing, while Israeli media reported that the Shin Bet domestic security service was involved.European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlersTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did the authorities say? Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander, said "an arrest operation was conducted before dawn" following "the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians." Foreign Minister ⁠Gideon Saar and the Israeli military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attacks on the diplomats. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" ⁠with the Israeli military. He added that the facts of the attack on ⁠Levine were "unclear." The attacks came ahead of the crucial October 27 elections for Netanyahu.West Bank olive harvest under attackTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will the Israeli settlers face prosecution? Settler violence against Palestinians has surged, with at least 170 attacks reported since September 27, according to Israeli human rights group Yesh Din. DW's correspondent in Jerusalem, Tania Kraemer, said Palestinians, journalists and international observers have little confidence that the arrests will lead to charges against the alleged perpetrators. Citing a study of Israeli police investigations into violence against Palestinians in the West Bank by Yesh Din, Kraemer said only about 3% of investigations between 2005 and 2023 ended in a full or partial conviction. More than 80% were closed because police failed to identify suspects or gather sufficient evidence, the Yesh Din report said. title: How AI is shaping Israel's election campaign
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OEgGNetanyahu's Likud has used AI in its campaign more than any other major partyImage: Ohad Zwigenberg/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture allianceAdvertisementIn a 19-second clipposted to X, Gadi Eisenkot, a candidate for prime minister, stands with his arms outstretched and a huge smile on his face. In slow motion, he runs through a meadow toward a person who resembles his son, wearing a shirt with the words "Israeli Unity." But Eisenkot sails past him and instead embraces Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab politician who leads the Ra'am party, running in the elections. The video was posted on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's account. Opinion pollsshow Netanyahu and Eisenkot, who also happens to be a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, in a tight race. The AI-generated video appears to be designed to play on anti-Arab sentiment — a big part of Netanyahu's campaign. The clip was viewed more than 1 million times and stirred outrage. Eisenkot's son was killed in 2023 during the Israel-Hamas war. According to Ze Be AI, a research project of the Open University of Israel, monitoring AI content in the 2026 legislative election campaign, this clip is just one of more than 1,800 posts with AI-generated content that Netanyahu's Likud party had released throughout the election campaign by mid-October. That represents about a quarter of the Likud party social media materials analyzed by Ze Be AI. Netanyahu posted this AI-generated clip of rival Gadi Eisenkot on X in July. It was viewed more than 1 million timesImage: x.com/netanyahu On October 27, Israelis will vote in an election that could oust Netanyahu from power or cement his grip on the country for the coming years. Political scientists are already calling it Israel's first AI election. Parties have been deploying AI across every aspect of campaigning — from creating outrageous videos aimed at stirring controversy to robocalling voters and unleashing bots online. "There is a scenario where, in a strategic point shortly before the election, AI could or would be used in ways that would steer controversy that could tilt the election results," said Anat Ben-David, a media researcher leading the Ze Be AI project at the Open University of Israel. AI videos go mainstream Ben-David and her research team have been tracking all of the content posted on social media by politicians since the end of July. By mid-October, they had collected more than 44,000 posts across Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok and found that over 14% of the material used AI in some way. A hybrid approach was most common, with AI being deployed for a part or segments of an ad: in images, music, subtitles, logos or full-fledged deepfakes. Some fringe parties use the greatest ratio of AI in their content. But Likud is the winner by far when it comes to sheer numbers of AI use in content analyzed by the team. Netanyahu's party is followed his left-wing rivals, the Democrats, and then Eisenkot's party, Yashar — though at far lower numbers. Israel's Central Elections Committee issued a new rule in July mandating that all AI-generated or -manipulated content in election campaigning be labeled. Beyond that, there are few limits. "There's no AI Act, no Digital Services Act, and the privacy law is very outdated," Ben-David said. "Then you see new [AI] uses that would be impossible to see in Europe." Some of those uses have come from Israel's most prominent politicians. Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, has been trying to capitalize on popular internet trends. One videolabeled as AI content features him sitting under a ceiling fan — with each rotation of the blade, his outfit changes: from an army uniform to a T-shirt with the popular slogan "bring them home now" (referring to Israeli hostages in Gaza) to a suit and tie. In one photorealistic AI video, posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in September, Israel's attorney general and Supreme Court justices are apprehended at an anti-government protest. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara has frequently clashed with the ruling coalition. An AI-generated video posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich shows Israel’s attorney general and Supreme Court justices being detained at an anti-government protestImage: x.com/bezalelsm And National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir shared an AI-generated video of Palestinians being wheeled on a conveyor belt into what looks like a concentration camp. That post drew widespread condemnation, with Germany's Foreign Ministry calling it"completely unacceptable" and "abhorrent." The election authority has shown some willingness to intervene. In July, its chairman ordered Smotrich to take down an unlabeled AI video it called misleading. A new generation of robocall It's not just deepfakes and ads: AI is also being used to reach voters directly. Some voters are getting a new kind of AI-powered robocall — far more conversational than the robotic automated calls of the past. Nitsan Yasur, a disinformation researcher at the Israel InternetAssociation, shared a recording with DW of a four-minute phone call. Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the pollsTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 videoIn it, a voice introduces itself as a pollster named Danielle with an Israeli polling institute and asks for his voting preferences. When Yasur asks if the voice is human, it admits, "there is no human agent on the line," before continuing to ask, "would you like to continue with the short survey?" The bot fields several of Yasur's questions, while always steering back to who he would vote for. But when Yasur asks five times who commissioned the survey, it doesn't reveal the information. So it remains unclear whether this was part of an election campaign or a poll. What is clear is how advanced robocalling has become. "You don't need real people making real phone calls, which are obviously limited in time and capacity," Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, a senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told DW. Efforts to shape what chatbots tell voters Some Israelis are also turning to AI for advice on how to vote. About a quarter of Israelis said they would consider using AI tools or other online services to inform their voting decisions, the Israel Internet Association found in a survey. That raises concerns about generative engine optimization (GEO): creating online content designed to be picked up by AI chatbots and shape their answers. The Israeli government has already tapped this industry. According to filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, it paid a US firm to build websites meant to feed LLM systems with content supportive of the government in order to make AI chatbots more pro-Israel. "The same industries are going to be used now inwards in order to affect the elections," she said. Bot accounts promote Netanyahu online There's fake content, and then there are fake audiences. Scooper, an Israeli company specializing in media monitoring, told DW that it discovered a network of inauthentic accounts boosting Netanyahu on social media. On X, more than 1,000 new accounts have been appearing daily and immediately following the Israeli prime minister. His Instagram following has also surged in recent weeks. About 70% of the accounts that share Netanyahu's posts on X are based outside of Israel and resemble bots, Scooper research manager Gil Feldman told DW. Feldman said the company flagged them by looking for suspicious behavior such as round-the-clock posting, recent creation dates and missing profile pictures. Israelis demand accountability for October 7To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 videoAnd it's not just Netanyahu: The Israeli watchdog FakeReporter found a bot campaign linked to Ben-Gvir's campaign, which his office denied. FakeReporter discovered a network of more than 100 accounts, some using AI-generated images and identities, targeting Smotrich and others. Though bot networks are nothing new, AI can make them cheaper and easier to run. And, because Israelis are early and eager adopters of new technology, Shwartz Altshuler sees the country as a test case for how AI is reshaping elections around the world. "The whole machinery of political propaganda is becoming totally different," Shwartz Altshuler said. Edited by: Uta Steinwehr, Chiponda Chimbelu, Joscha Weber, Shani Rozanes Advertisement

content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OOOwGermany is hoping for more investment in the high-tech sector, among other thingsImage: Sylvio Dittrich/IMAGOAdvertisementSkip next section What you need to knowWhat you need to know Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to give the welcome speech at a conference aiming to boost investment in Germany Operations have returned to normal after a security incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport Carmaker Volkswagen is intending to freeze the salaries of many of its workers until 2030 The Berlin Social Democrats and Greens are to decide whether to start coalition negotiations with the Left Party after ending exploratory talks This is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on Monday, October 19, 2026: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Skip next section Foreign Ministry summons Iranian ambassador over planned anti-Israel attacks10/19/2026October 19, 2026Foreign Ministry summons Iranian ambassador over planned anti-Israel attacksTimothy JonesThe Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran. "We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X. "We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote. A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG). In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of Schuster and Beck. The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force. The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations. https://p.dw.com/p/5OPbRSkip next section Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: Police10/19/2026October 19, 2026Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: PoliceTimothy JonesThe breach in the fence triggered a major police operationImage: Erik-Holm Langhof/EHL Media/dpa/picture allianceTwo men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday. The two, aged 20 and 32, have handed themselves in to police. The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi. The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes. German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied. https://p.dw.com/p/5OPSLSkip next section German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo Institute10/19/2026October 19, 2026German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo InstituteTimothy Jones German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank. The figure represents a 7.1% decline. Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%. But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions. At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo. It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes. Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany. "Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said. "The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future." https://p.dw.com/p/5OOzJSkip next section German woman climber dies in fall in Italy10/19/2026October 19, 2026German woman climber dies in fall in ItalyTimothy JonesA German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday. title: Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro clash in heated presidential debate
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OOQ0In a tense moment, Lula challenged Bolsonaro for both of them to open their personal finances to scrutinyImage: Jean Carniel/REUTERSAdvertisementBrazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday had a heated exchange during their first face-to-face presidential debate. The televised debate, which saw the candidates trade insults and accusations, came a week before the October 25 presidential runoff. Bolsonaro finished nearly two points ahead of Lula in the election's first round earlier this month. How did the presidential debate turn heated? The contentious debate focused on the economy, public security, corruption and Brazil's relations with the United States, before it devolved into personal attacks. Bolsonaro criticized Lula over the cost of living, public security and social spending, accusing him of spending recklessly to secure re-election. Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug," alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups. "Lying is ​the Bolsonaro family's strong suit," Lula said. Bolsonaro retaliated by accusing Lula of being tainted by corruption, saying during the debate that it was better he maintains a distance "because my wallet could be stolen." "Brazil is going to retire you," Bolsonaro told Lula. Meanwhile, Lula also brought up the populist Senator's ties to US President Donald Trump. "It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula, accusing Bolsonaro of conspiring to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals to the US. Flavio's father also came up during the discussion. Former President Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt after his failed 2022 re-election bid. The next presidential debate is scheduled for Friday, October 23.Brazilian politics have been increasingly polarized for nearly a decadeImage: Miguel Schincariol/AFP Thousands rally in support Meanwhile, tens of thousands of supporters of both candidates rallied in cities across Brazil ahead of the debate, flooding the streets of Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and other cities. In Sao Paulo, Bolsonaro's supporters called for the release of Jair Bolsonaro. On the other hand, at Rio's Copacabana Beach, Lula supporters led a "rally for democracy." There were similar events in Brasilia and 16 other state capitals. title: Macron slams 'failures' over protest unrest in France but refuses his interior minister's resignation
content: https://p.dw.com/p/5OORECity authorities have accused French police of being unprepared Image: Guillaume Saligot/AFPAdvertisementFrance's President Emmanuel Macron has condemned the "failures in anticipation and intelligence" by French authorities, the Elysee Palace said Monday, after nationwide cost-of-living protests were marred by violence. Despite the failures, Macron has refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, the presidential palace added. Macron and his government are under pressure from opposition politicians, who have called for Nunez to be removed, after mass rallies on Saturday over the rising cost of living and high fuel costs turned violent. In some of the worst urban violence France has seen in years, nearly 2,400 people were arrested, while almost 1,000 police and gendarmes (French armed police) were injured, the Interior Ministry said Sunday. Interior minister: Police 'lost control' of situation Nunez on Monday admitted that police across the country had "lost control" of the situation over the weekend. As tens of thousands of people took to streets across the country to protest rising costs and social inequality, crowds of mostly masked and mostly male youths clashed with police, looting shops and torching public and private property, including the historic Limoges city hall.Macron has vowed a tough response to the unrest, which saw Limoges city hall set ablazeImage: Melaine Payzal/AFP Nunez agreed with Macron over what he called authorities' "lack of anticipation," saying he tendered his resignation "because I felt responsible for everything that happened." Macron has instructed Nunez to "take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence," according to a statement from his office. The president also ordered Nunez to "put in place new operational methods for security forces" to handle the crisis — and how to deal with violent looters — moving forward. In an effort to quell the situation, authorities in the southern city of Marseille announced a ban on Monday on all "gatherings and demonstrations" from noon to 8 pm. Nunez is expected to visit France's second-largest city later on Monday.President Macron urges distinction between protesters and vandalsTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video French PM calls for partial curfews Prime ⁠Minister Sebastien ⁠Lecornu, meanwhile, has called for some local municipalities ‌to ​impose "very limited" and "localized" curfews in cities around the country to curb further unrest. But Lecornu said there were currently no plans to cancel Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League home match against Barcelona on Tuesday night. After a Monday crisis meeting, Lecornu said "I am absolutely determined to restore order," adding that he would not rule out imposing a state of emergency, "If needed, I will do it." "As things stand," he continued, "the issue of curfews, and the implementation of those curfews, seems better suited to the situation we may be facing." Elsewhere in the French capital on Monday, a group of students blocked the entrance to the Louvre in solidarity with the protesters, with unions adding that the famous museum would remain closed. Students were also blockading the Sciences Po university in the center of the city.People in Paris walk past vehicles that were set on fire during Saturday's unrestImage: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance How large were the protests and the police deployment? Organizers, hoping to revive the momentum of the 2018-2019 "Yellow Vest" movement that challenged Macron during his first term, called the protests just six months before the country is set to elect his replacement. This weekend's mobilization called on students, workers, retirees, farmers, climate activists and anti-fascists to take to the streets and voice their dissatisfaction with the country's economic and social outlook. France's CGT union put nationwide turnout at 500,000. Initially it was reported that only 10,000 police and gendarmes had been deployed nationwide. But the Interior Ministry quickly corrected that tally, saying that 60,000 had been mobilized ahead of the protests, including 5,000 in Paris. Paris deployed 14,000 police and gendarmes in Paris alone during a recent high-profile visit by Pope Leo XIV, when as many as 700,000 people gathered in the center of the capital to hear the pontiff deliver Mass.Violent unrest rocks France after nationwide protestsTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Macron's opponents looking to assign blame Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed ("La France Insoumise", or LFI) party and a perennial presidential candidate, attended the rally in Paris on Saturday. Melenchon has criticized media coverage of the unrest, stressing that most demonstrations had been peaceful. His rival Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally (RN) accused him of "legitimizing violence" and seeking to "plunge the country into chaos." Le Pen's political ally and successor as RN leader, Jordan Bardella, described those responsible for the violence as "professionals of chaos" and accused the far left of discrediting legitimate social demands. Benoit Payan, the left-wing mayor of Marseille, slammed violent protesters using the event as an excuse to destroy property and attack police in remarks to French outlet BFMTV, saying, "It is unacceptable to use this type of claim to enter, break and destroy the foundations that unite us as a nation." Payan described violent protesters as "useful idiots of the far right."France protests escalate as unrest spreads across citiesTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.
