The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.Explore more on these topicsChinese economyChinaEconomicsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivals
content: The Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest. Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest. Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesThree deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivalsDeputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhereThere is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.View image in fullscreenParticipants push and pull a float during the Danjiri festival celebrations in Anan, Tokushima. Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockThe accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known as yarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.View image in fullscreenThe floats weigh up to 4 tonnes each. Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockSaijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed in fundoshi loincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.Explore more on these topicsJapanAsia PacificFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
content: Amelia Earhart in the cockpit of a plane in 1931. She and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished on 2 July 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveView image in fullscreenAmelia Earhart in the cockpit of a plane in 1931. She and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished on 2 July 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveAmelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of treesExpedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited islandA US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance Read morePrevious visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.Map showing location of Nikumaroro IslandBy Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed Read moreIt said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.Explore more on these topicsAmelia EarhartPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
content: An electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/ReutersNo 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU schemeBeijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe packageNo 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said. Explore more on these topicsTrade policyElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsInternational tradeLabourChinaChinese economyTariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
content: Aerial view from a plane wing of Nikumaroro’s lagoon and forested coastline taken during a 1938 aerial survey, when it was known as Gardner Island. Photograph: RNZAFView image in fullscreenAerial view from a plane wing of Nikumaroro’s lagoon and forested coastline taken during a 1938 aerial survey, when it was known as Gardner Island. Photograph: RNZAFMuseum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearanceA New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.View image in fullscreenOne of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF OfficialEarhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.View image in fullscreenAmelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937. Photograph: AlamyThis week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.Explore more on these topicsAmelia EarhartNew ZealandPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ellie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mine
content: Ellie Goulding attended the opening of a Boodles store in London and modelled the brand’s diamond jewellery. Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesView image in fullscreenEllie Goulding attended the opening of a Boodles store in London and modelled the brand’s diamond jewellery. Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesEllie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mineSinger ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous landThe singer Ellie Goulding has admitted her error at having promoted diamonds at the centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land in Australia, despite having spent years campaigning on environmental issues – including the effects of mining on ancestral lands.She appeared at a event in London earlier this month for the jewellery brand Boodles, modelling some of its newly acquired pink diamonds, some of which came from a controversial mine in Western Australia.“Protecting the environment is a cause close to my heart. I always strive to uphold those values. Regretfully, in this instance, I fell short,” said Goulding, who was made an MBE for services to biodiversity and the climate last year. “I was not aware of the concerns surrounding the Argyle mine and I am grateful that it has been brought to my attention.“You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again. The Indigenous and local communities affected deserve better. While I am mortified to have made this error in judgment, I am letting this moment serve as a reminder and an opportunity to continue to question the status quo, to learn and do better.”View image in fullscreen‘You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again,’ Goulding said. Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesAs well as serving as a global goodwill ambassador for the UN environment programme, Goulding is an ambassador for the environmental organisation WWF, which said it “takes seriously the environmental impact of mining and the effect it can have on Indigenous and local communities”.The charity added: “Ellie is a passionate advocate for nature and human rights and has championed the rights of Indigenous peoples as a WWF ambassador. We have discussed this issue with Ellie and continue to value her support.”A week before the Boodles event in London, it was announced the firm had bought the Argyle Pink Diamonds brand, as well as its inventory, from the mining firm Rio Tinto. A source close to Goulding suggested this timing may have led to the singer falling short of her own environmental values.View image in fullscreenThe Argyle diamond mine in the Kimberley region of Western Australia. Mining ended there in 2020. Photograph: Murray Rayner/Nature Publishing Group/AFP/Getty ImagesAccording to the Daily Mirror, which first reported the news, the Gelganyem Group, which represents the traditional owners of the land that was mined for the diamonds, has expressed concerns about the state it has been left in by the industrial processes now the mining has ceased.The group told the paper: “Gelganyem chair Kia Dowell, a Gija woman, acknowledges Ellie Goulding’s apology and welcomes her recognition that Indigenous and local communities deserve better. She hopes it helps the public and Rio Tinto shareholders understand what is at stake at Argyle and the standard Rio Tinto’s mine closure must meet.”The paper quoted the organisation’s representative as saying traditional owners wanted “unrestricted access without unresolved risks being left for future generations”, adding that Pfas – or forever chemicals – were one of “several technical issues traditional owners, Gelganyem and independent experts have raised”.Rio Tinto said: “Mining at Argyle in Western Australia ended in 2020 after 37 years, and we are currently undertaking major mine closure works, including rehabilitation, with long-term monitoring and maintenance to follow. We acknowledge traditional owners as custodians of country. We are continuing to talk to them and their representatives, the Gelganyem Group, about closure, including Pfas.”Boodles has not responded to a request for comment. The Mirror quoted a source close to the firm as saying it was not responsible for the mine itself and adding: “Boodles have bought the last batch of pink diamonds and assets from Rio Tinto including their website and Instagram account. Other jewellers have used pink diamonds in their collections.”Explore more on these topicsEllie GouldingMining (Environment)Indigenous AustraliansRio TintoWestern AustraliaMining (Business)Fashion industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injured
content: Helen Haines has been injured in an incident outside her office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHelen Haines has been injured in an incident outside her office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injuredAnthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? What we know so far Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a man was in custody after the alleged attack on Haines that was now being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce.He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police.Helen Haines is in a critical condition after an alleged attack. Here’s what we know so farRead more“Helen Haines is incredibly hard-working. She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her, she is a well-loved member of her community, and this will come as an incredible shock to that community,” Albanese said.He said he respected her integrity most of all.“It doesn’t mean we always agree, but I always agree that her motives are good,” Albanese said.“Our thoughts remain with Helen Haines at this very difficult time.”View image in fullscreenABC vision from the scene near where Helen Haines was allegedly struck by a vehicle. Photograph: ABCThe prime minister and Victoria police said they were not aware of any recent direct threats to Haines.Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019.Albanese later said on the ABC’s 7.30 program that while he did not want to speculate on the motivation for the alleged attack, he had repeatedly warned “the temperature has increased in recent times” in relation to politics.He had feared that would increase the risk of political violence occurring in Australia that had been seen in other western democracies.Albanese, who became emotional at times during the interview, said he first was told that Haines had been injured in a car accident, before being informed it was allegedly a deliberate act.“This wasn’t an accident,” he said. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also said there had been an increase in threats towards politicians.“The year before last, we had 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against various high officeholders,” he said.“The more recent financial year, that 951 has gone to 1,067.”‘Our beloved Helen’In a statement, Haines’s family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance.“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement.“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.“Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.“Please keep Helen in your thoughts.”Wangaratta map Haines was airlifted to hospital in Melbourne.In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car.The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition.“Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.”Police said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”.Speaking at the scene, acting Supt Ashley Mason said it was being treated as an isolated incident.He said that the bystanders who assisted in the arrest and with Haines should be commended for acting as they did when confronted with a “horrific tragic incident”.It was a “dynamic incident” with an extensive crime scene, he said.‘Deeply appalled’The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said he knew the alleged attack would be devastating for the Wangaratta community and all those Haines represented.“I am deeply appalled by this [alleged] violent attack on Helen Haines,” he said in a statement.“My thoughts – and the thoughts of all Victorians – are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community.”The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said t political attacks cannot be normalised in Australia.Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?Read moreThe Liberal leader said he was “deeply saddened and distressed” and was praying for Haines and her family.“This is a shocking day for our nation ... Australians will be angry and appalled by the [alleged] attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he said in a statement on social media.In a social media post, the Nationals MP Michael McCormack said it was “such awful news”.“Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said.‘Politically motivated violence’Asio has in recent years repeatedly warned about the rising threat of politically motivated violence.“Political differences, political debates and political protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy,” Mike Burgess, the Asio director general, said in 2025.“Unfortunately, here and overseas, levels of personal grievance and frustration are growing.“Rightly or wrongly some Australians feel dispossessed, disaffected, disenfranchised ... many of the aggrieved do not necessarily espouse violent views, but may still see violence as a legitimate way to effect political or societal change.”He added last year that although Australia’s terrorism threat level remained at probable, the system was not “designed for a situation like the one we now face”.“We do know the environment is degrading and acts of politically motivated violence are becoming more likely than probable suggests,” he said.“Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack.”Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesAustralian politicsVictoriaIndependentsAustralian security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier ‘deeply appalled’ after Indi MP Haines injured – as it happened
content: We are closing the blog for the night.You can read the full story on the alleged attack on Helen Haines here, and an explainer here.We’ll be back first thing tomorrow, until then, here is a rundown of what we know so far: The independent MP for Indi is in a critical condition after an alleged attack involving a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, at about 3.35pm. A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee is in custody, and the alleged attack is being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. The motive is not yet known. A knife was allegedly found in his car after he was detained by a passerby when he exited his vehicle. Well-wishes towards Haines have flowed in from across the political spectrum. The prime minister held a snap press conference on Monday evening where he described Haines, who has represented Indi since 2019, as a “thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across parliament”. The opposition leader, the Greens leader David Shoebridge, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and a string of independent and Nationals MPs have also sent their thoughts to Haines and her family, with many describing Haines as representing “the very best” in parliament. Thoughts and prayers for Haines came amid calls to lower the political temperature in Australia. Nationals MP in the neighbouring electorate of Nicholls, Sam Birrell, said the way people were engaging had become “more angry and heated”, and added the alleged attack should be a “wake-up call”. Addressing the media in Wangaratta, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said police were still investigating whether the incident was targeted. He said there was no ongoing threat to the community and nothing to indicate the parties were known to each other.

title: Pregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report finds
content: The number of pregnancy discrimination complaints to the human rights commission has increased from 52 in 2023 to 71 last year. Photograph: damircudic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe number of pregnancy discrimination complaints to the human rights commission has increased from 52 in 2023 to 71 last year. Photograph: damircudic/Getty ImagesPregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report findsSex discrimination commissioner says too often ‘it’s the woman who has the burden of bringing a complaint’ in parental discrimination cases Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast Women are being forced out of employment through “sham redundancies”, losing shifts and facing hostile work environments after having a baby, according to a report by the Australian Human Rights Commission, which warns parental discrimination remains a major barrier to gender equality.The commission’s report suggests pregnancy discrimination is more prominent for vulnerable groups, including immigrant and First Nations women, people with disability and LGBTQ+ people. The commission held roundtables with dozens of parents, legal and community advocates when compiling the report.In one case study detailed in the Balancing Act report, Luisa*, an experienced HR manager in the healthcare industry, was made redundant one month after telling her employer she was pregnant.“Her employer questioned who would support Luisa after the baby was born, because her family lived overseas,” the report noted. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “Luisa explained that her husband would take parental leave and that she planned to return to work soon after the birth. Luisa also offered to continue working on a part-time basis, but the redundancy went ahead.”The sex discrimination commissioner, Anna Cody, said urgent law reform was needed to the sex discrimination act to protect women and families, arguing legislation has not kept pace with a changing society. She said women delayed telling their employers about pregnancies for fear of losing work.“Frequently, when a woman does tell that she is pregnant ... she will experience either performance management, or suddenly – if she’s in insecure work, and we know that migrant women and women targeted by racism are more likely to be an insecure and shift work – then the shifts will dry up,” Cody said.“The third thing that happens is redundancies – and they are ‘sham redundancies’. They’re not ... because the job is no longer required or has been eliminated within the workplace, it’s because they no longer want that woman working in the job because she’s pregnant and is going to leave.”A 2014 national review by the AHRC found 49% of mothers reported discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or on their return to work.Cody said discrimination remained widespread but it was hard to know whether the situation had improved. The commission would push the federal government to fund another survey, she said.The chief executive of the Parenthood, Georgie Dent, told the national press club in September that another survey was critical.“It must be reinstated,” she said at the time. “We can’t fix what we’ve stopped counting.”Being a working parent is a logistical nightmare. Imagine if school holidays were something we looked forward to | Emily MulliganRead moreA 2024 survey of 1,048 parent workers by the University of South Australia found 89% reported discrimination during pregnancy, 85% reported experiencing discrimination while on parental leave and 92% reported discrimination when returning to work.The number of complaints to the human rights commission has increased from 52 in 2023 to 71 in 2025. Cody said complaints to the Fair Work Commission were higher but many parents didn’t report discrimination.“If you make the loss of a job look like a redundancy, the employer is the one who has all the evidence to show whether or not the job has actually disappeared, and yet it’s the complainant, it’s the woman, who has the responsibility, that burden, of bringing a complaint,” Cody said.“We know that when women are having their child, or are pregnant, that’s a really vulnerable time. And so then to put on top of that, ‘Now it’s your responsibility to make a complaint to either the Fair Work Commission or to the Australian Human Rights Commission,’ sometimes that’s just too much.”The AHRC takes up to a year to allocate a conciliator after a complaint is lodged, meaning there is a backlog of cases.The commission’s report, to be released this week, found some parents were given less responsibility at work after the birth of a child. Others were given fewer shifts or no opportunity for development.New parents faced difficulty asking for flexibility and safe arrangements for breastfeeding.Another case study, Michelle, told the AHRC she lost her job after asking to work longer shifts rather than multiple shorter shifts to care for her two young children and terminally ill father.“Her workplace responded to her request by no longer offering her any shifts and dismissed her from her role,” the report wrote.Meanwhile, Emily told the commission she was discouraged from taking lactation breaks while employed at a tech start-up despite its clean, accessible and secure breastfeeding area.“She was expected to work uninterrupted, long hours and was unable to take her lactation breaks. Despite the available space and policies, the culture and attitudes in her workplace made Emily feel unsupported and led her to stop breastfeeding her child earlier than she wanted to.”*Name changed by human rights commission in its reportExplore more on these topicsAustralia newsIndustrial relationsHuman rightsWomenPregnancynewsShareReuse this content

title: Mother assessed as posing no immediate risk to others three weeks before Elizabeth Struhs’ manslaughter, inquest hears
content: Kerrie Struhs’ eight-year-old daughter Elizabeth (pictured) died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents. Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenKerrie Struhs’ eight-year-old daughter Elizabeth (pictured) died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents. Photograph: BBCMother assessed as posing no immediate risk to others three weeks before Elizabeth Struhs’ manslaughter, inquest hearsQueensland correctional services officer did not have access to details of Kerrie Struhs’ past offending which included child neglect Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Elizabeth Struhs’ mother, Kerrie, was assessed by correctional services as being of no immediate risk to others by an officer who had no access to her offending history, three weeks before she and others caused her eight-year-old daughter to die, a Brisbane inquest has heard.Kerrie Struhs was sentenced to five months’ jail for child neglect after failing to take Elizabeth to hospital to treat her type 1 diabetes in 2019. Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard has previously heard that Elizabeth was so unwell when she presented at hospital that she was nearly dead, and was in a coma.Elizabeth was discharged from hospital into the care of her father, Jason Struhs, by the department of child safety. Jason was later also convicted for child neglect over the 2019 incident.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhen Kerrie was released from jail on 16 December 2021 on court-ordered parole, she was assessed by two different correctional officers, the inquest heard on Monday.Elizabeth died just 22 days later of diabetic ketoacidosis, after Jason stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland.Kerrie met with a parole intake officer the day of her release from prison in 2021.That officer told the court that she didn’t have access to the QP9 for Kerrie’s conviction – a file produced by prosecutors and the police that would have included details about her offence – or the judge’s sentencing remarks.She also had no other knowledge of Kerrie before the meeting, but was able to access some details online, including her offence type.The court later heard that the other information was not accessible due to an administrative error.Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hearsRead moreThe parole intake officer conducted an “immediate risk assessment” of Kerrie at the meeting.The court was shown the file, which include the question: “Has the offender described any issues that may pose an immediate risk to themselves, others or impact on their immediate management?”The officer marked this “no”.A child safety officer had previously marked Elizabeth as “safe” just days after her 2019 admission to hospital.The file containing the risk assessment also disclosed a conversation between Kerrie and the parole intake officer about her 2019 offence.“Kerrie said she believed that God would heal the child but she wouldn’t interfere with someone else getting the child treatment ...” the officer reported, in contemporaneous notes presented to the court.“She said she would do the same again. She said that she would keep that trust in God that he would heal.”Kerrie had previously made similar remarks to healthcare workers, child safety officers, police and others. Brisbane-based specialist doctors considered her beliefs so dangerous that Elizabeth could not safely live in the same home as her, but were overruled by child safety.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionA senior correctional services officer told the court Kerrie should have been flagged for the “serious offenders unit” due to causing “serious child harm”.That would have led to additional oversight over her case, the officer said.Kerrie’s parole intake officer told the court she upgraded her level of risk from “low” to “standard” due to the seriousness of her offence, which meant Kerrie would have to meet with a parole officer weekly.She also booked her another in-person meeting with a different parole officer, on 23 December.The officer who met her on 23 December said she met with Kerrie for just 10 or 15 minutes and didn’t take the same steps she might have at any other time of the year, two days before Christmas.Both officers were duty officers, filling in for others.Kerrie was also scheduled to meet with a parole officer a third time, on 6 January 2022.Elizabeth died on 7 January after Jason withdrew her insulin from 3 January 2022.Kerrie, Jason and the other 12 adult members of the religious sect they were members of were convicted of manslaughter over Elizabeth’s death last year.None of the witnesses in the coronial inquest can be identified, for legal reasons.The inquest continues.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: French PM blames ‘ultra-left’ for exploiting protests as he seeks partial curfews – Europe live
content: French PM Lecornu says he has asked prefects to implement “a number of partial curfews” in certain “localised” urban areas to stop further disorder, which he attributes to “the extreme-left” and some criminal elements.France’s prime minister Sébastien Lecornu looks on before an emergency meeting in Paris. Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesWe will no doubt hear more on this from local authorities, as in the example of Marseille (10:32).He also says the government is determined to respond to the events as needed, and if declaring a state of emergency is deemed necessary, they would do so – but that’s a major decision to make and currently not being considered.He says be believes “there is an agenda of chaos being pushed by the far-left,” with the intention of disrupting next year’s presidential election, and that’s why he urges the NR leaders to attend his briefing later today, despite their plans no to do so (12:20).Lecornu also says that there will be a “strong” response from the country’s judiciary, cracking down on the violence and crime on the margins of the protests. Investigators are also looking through social media footage, where rioters often did not wear masks.New measures to stop riots from reoccurring will be put in place starting tonight, but tomorrow’s football game between PSG and Barcelona is currently scheduled to still go ahead.He also says that furlough measures for businesses affected by riots will kick in on Tuesday to ensure all jobs are saved despite any disruption to business operations in the build up to the busy Christmas period.He says there will also be further targeted measures, but with little detail at this stage.Separately, the government will also push to expedite various assessments required to pay out any insurance claims.Lecornu also says that the right to legitimate protest needs to be safeguarded and considered separately from the riots and clashes with police forces.

title: French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots
content: Rioting and looting continued around the country on Sunday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenRioting and looting continued around the country on Sunday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersFrench prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riotsInterior minister concedes police ‘lost control’, with forces in cities including Paris and Lyon overwhelmed after ‘lack of anticipation’ Europe live – latest updates France’s prime minister has said he has asked regional authorities to impose partial curfews in some cities after the government admitted police had “lost control” in several places during violent weekend protests around the country.Sébastien Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities such as Paris, he added.Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”. He did not say which cities, or what form the curfews would take.His comments came after France’s interior minister conceded police “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.View image in fullscreenLaurent Nuñez, the interior minister, offered his resignation to Emmanuel Macron, which was declined. Photograph: Julien de Rosa/Pool AFP/APThe protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said. Nearly 2,400 people – 70% of them adults – were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence, he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.View image in fullscreenAn estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted across France during the rioting. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesMacron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.View image in fullscreenThe Louvre was unable to open as scheduled on Monday because of protesters blocking its entrance. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersOn Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestEmmanuel MacronParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
content: Workers repair railway tracks at a metro station hit by an overnight Russian missile strike on Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenWorkers repair railway tracks at a metro station hit by an overnight Russian missile strike on Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUS gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy saysUkrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in ongoing row with Trump over apparent support for MoscowUkraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence in order to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at around 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.Ukraine did receive a warning before a successive strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him ... he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”For years, the US had warned Ukraine before Russia launches ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeTrump administrationVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpKyivnewsShareReuse this content

title: France hit by debt sell-off as protests unnerve investors
content: A town hall in the French city of Limoges was set on fire during the protests. Photograph: SDIS 87/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA town hall in the French city of Limoges was set on fire during the protests. Photograph: SDIS 87/AFP/Getty ImagesFrance hit by debt sell-off as protests unnerve investorsDifference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs widens after violence breaks out Business live – latest updates France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops looted and thousands of arrests across the country.Almost 2,400 people have been arrested in France, the interior ministry said on Sunday, with police deploying teargas in confrontations with protesters.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, condemned the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.“Looking at these images, we all asked ourselves: what is going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” he said.The chaos has spooked investors in France’s government debt, with the yield on its 10-year yield rising by 10 basis points to 4.89% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall.This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards the highest levels seen in 14 years.Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the Euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation,” the analyst added.The two-year French bond yield rose by eight basis points to 3.63%.Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, with sterling rising to €1.188.Violence erupted across France after weeks of peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living.While tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs [French government bonds]”.He said: “With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.”The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by five basis points to 5.42%.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionThe rise in borrowing costs will add further strain to France’s public finances, as the government also tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively.The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. However, there are growing fears that political pressure could derail these plans, which could push up borrowing and add more to the country’s debt pile.The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% in early trading on Monday, falling to $1.1197.The French Cac 40, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.2% in morning trading, compared with a 0.7% drop on the pan-European Stoxx Europe 600 index.French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 2%.Explore more on these topicsFranceBondsStock marketsEuropeProtestEuroCost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Monday briefing: What you need to know about a weekend of chaos in France
content: Limoges city hall was destroyed over a weekend of protests and riots. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLimoges city hall was destroyed over a weekend of protests and riots. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty ImagesMonday briefing: What you need to know about a weekend of chaos in FranceIn today’s newsletter: Violent riots and looting have dominated the headlines, but the unrest gripping the country and beyond reflects deeper public anger over everyday issuesGood morning. I bet your weekend was better than Emmanuel Macron’s. On Friday, the evening before mass protests that were planned across France, he attended a Céline Dion concert in Paris with his wife, Brigitte, prompting comparisons to Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette. On Sunday evening, he was forced to give a televised speech condemning the “unbridled violence” and riots that erupted in French cities over the weekend.The rioters that burned makeshift barricades of bicycles in Paris, destroyed the steeple of Limoges’ town hall and set fire to Lyon’s tourism office were described as “LE CHAOS” on the front page of La Tribune Dimanche, and “SCENES D’INSURRECTION” on Le Parisien Dimanche. By Sunday, protests had also taken place in Spain, Portugal and Italy.Today’s newsletter explains what happened in France over the weekend, and why this crisis threatens to engulf Macron’s government. First, here are the weekend’s headlines.Weekend roundup The Vatican | Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung. UK news | A “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him. US politics | Donald Trump fired his immediately embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, on Friday evening after just five days in the job. The conservative commentator becomes the shortest serving occupant of the role in US history. Reform | A Reform UK mayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff. Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police. Energy | The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies. In depth: ‘Gen Z is really facing a polycrisis of different issues’View image in fullscreenMost of the protests were peaceful marches calling for change. Photograph: Geoffroy van der Hasselt/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the early hours of Sunday, cleaners started to remove the detritus from Parisian streets: shards of glass from broken shop windows, smashed bus shelters, burned out cars. The smell of teargas still lingered in the Métro station at Place de la République. “Areas of Paris looked like a wasteland,” Paolo Stuppia, a sociologist at Sciences Po in Paris, tells me. About 855 people have been arrested in Paris, and a total of 2,400 have been arrested across France. Lamia El Aaraje, the Socialist deputy mayor of Paris, said the capital had experienced a level of violence “we had never seen before.”There have been so many incredible images of destruction (see our gallery here) that it’s possible to forget Saturday was, for the most part, defined by peaceful protests. Hundreds of thousands of people, many of them schoolchildren and parents, joined marches across the country. A far smaller group of protesters, many wearing face masks, smashed street furniture and torched cars and bus stops. A third group took the opportunity to loot shops. “I saw teenagers running off with shoeboxes, clothes, and perfume,” Angelique Chrisafis, the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, tells me.It’s the second group that has dominated the headlines. On Saturday afternoon, people set the town hall in Limoges alight (its spire collapsed dramatically on Saturday evening), and broke into the city hall in Marseille. “It wasn’t as if the peaceful protesters suddenly turned violent,” Chrisafis says. “It was as if the government didn’t have a hold on the situation, and suddenly, the police were really caught off guard.”The peaceful protesters ‘Our future is being stolen from us’When a small number of people break the law during otherwise peaceful protests, there’s a tendency to condemn such acts as “criminality, pure and simple” (to quote David Cameron during the 2011 London riots), and to disqualify the idea they represent a form of antagonism against authority. “If everything was going well in France, you wouldn’t have young kids ransacking stores,” Stuppia says.Such criminal acts can also become a means of undermining peaceful protesters. “Some of those people are now pretty upset because they believe the government will be talking about burning barricades rather than the fact they turned out in such large numbers,” Chrisafis says. French students have been protesting against the school system since September and calling for repairs to decrepit buildings, smaller class sizes, and reforms to a widely loathed university admissions system. Education is a particularly fraught subject in France, where academic credentials overwhelmingly determine job prospects. But their concerns are also broader; as Greta Thunberg put it recently, “our future is being stolen from us,” a feeling that many young people across the continent share.The student protests have since become the focus in a constellation of different issues, ranging from the cost of living to rising fuel prices and public service cuts. Those on Saturday drew in numerous groups, including unions and supporters of the Gilets Jaunes. “Gen-Z is really facing a polycrisis of different issues, from the climate crisis to the rise of the far right and the use of AI” Stuppia tells me. “And you can see the same set of issues coming alive in Italy, in Belgium, in Portugal, and with the Cockroach protests in India. Young people want change.” (You can read more about how these protests have spread to other European countries in this story by Sam Jones).The police ‘Entire cities ... left to the mercy of rioters’The police response has been at once strikingly brutal and remarkably inept. As Guardian columnist Rokhaya Diallo pointed out in this recent opinion piece, French schoolchildren have been “treated like enemies to be crushed” over the last few weeks. French lawyers have said that several teenagers have suffered “war-like” injuries from police, including a 14-year-old boy who suffered a fractured jaw and a 15-year-old whose hand was blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. The number of arrests has also been disproportionate: according to this graph by Pierre Bataille, a sociologist at Grenoble Alpes university, more people were arrested during two weeks of the student protests than members of the Gilets Jaunes were in an entire year.The shortcomings of this zealous focus on student protesters became clear on Saturday afternoon. Crowd psychologists have demonstrated that rather than instilling order, heavy-handed policing can actually trigger violence. While the police blocked a demonstration route between Place de la République and Place de la Concorde on Saturday citing “serious risks of public disorder,” large sections of Paris were left without enough officers to prevent looting. According to the French Green leader Marine Tondelier, “entire cities were left to the mercy of rioters, while peaceful protesters were subjected to violence.” She has since been calling for the resignation of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, calling his performance over the weekend “an absolute disaster”.The politicians ‘Social unrest is shaking our country’In his statement last night, Macron drew a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”, and criticised “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents” (pending an investigation, though, it’s impossible to say what the rioters’ motivations were). There are tricky and enduring questions that his government now faces. It failed to anticipate both the student protests that have engulfed France since September, and the violence that broke out over the weekend. As this interesting New Yorker piece (£) points out Macron’s experience of the public education system is limited, and even his education minister has admitted that at least some of his five children attend private schools.The protests and the police response have underscored how out of touch Macron’s government appears to be with French people, many of whom are angry about the price of fuel and the cost of living. This sense of disaster – described by the mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guérin, a member of the conservative Les Républicains party, as a “colossal failure of the state” – has overshadowed the thousands of people who turned out for peaceful protests, and plays into the hands of the far right (Marine Le Pen, who gave her own address on X before Macron’s, has described the riots as a “threat to democracy”). In a recent interview with Le Monde, the mayor of Lyon, Grégory Doucet, struck a more dispassionate tone, and said there need to be “concrete, political answers” to “the social unrest shaking our country.”The week to come Monday | The two-week biodiversity summit, Cop17, begins in Yerevan, Armenia, as countries come together to seek to protect nature. Tuesday | The Covid-19 inquiry publishes its report on the adult social care sector. Sunday | Incumbent Lula da Silva takes on Flavio Bolsonaro in the run-off of the Brazil general election. What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenLa Belle Dame sans Merci by Frank Dicksee. Photograph: Artepics/Alamy I enjoyed this piece from Sarah Clegg on the long history of romantasy fiction, with its origins in medieval romances which were apparently just as raunchy as today’s sexy page turners. Katy Vans, newsletters team Fascinating piece here from Anita Chaudhri on the rise of “competitive yoga”: new way to make the practice accessible, or a fundamental misunderstanding of its spirit? Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team This was an eye-opening piece; one of our reporters went undercover at a wellness conference in the UK to expose the dangerous health advice of Barbara O’Neill, who is seen as a risk to public safety in Australia. Katy SportView image in fullscreenNoni Madueke scored the only goal of the game. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianFootball | ​Arsenal left it late to snatch a 1-0 victory against Nottingham Forest at the City Ground, while Brighton had a resounding victory at home against Crystal Palace, winning 5-0 to put them 2nd in the Premier League. Elsewhere Man Utd could only manage a 1-1 draw away against Leeds.Cricket | The second test between South Africa and Australia was abandoned due to poor weather with only 12.2 overs being bowled.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionFootball | In the WSL Chelsea beat Spurs 6-2, putting pressure on league leaders Man City by moving up to 2nd place in the table.The front pagesView image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian“Macron condemns ‘unbridled violence’ of huge French riots”, is the Guardian’s front page today.The Times says “PM: Neets crisis is moral failure”, the Telegraph writes “Healey plans raid on family businesses”, the Express has “‘Axe the family farm tax now, prime minister,’” and the Mail leads with “True cost of Labour migration dithering”.The FT has “Investor anxiety and public backlash threaten to scupper $10tn AI boom”, Metro splashes “British kids in CRISIS” and the Sun says “Credit crunch”.Today in FocusView image in fullscreenEvan Gershkovich was working for the Wall Street Journal was detained, beaten and charged with espionage. Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesA spy charge, a Russian jail and a swap for an assassin: the story of Evan GershkovichUS journalist Evan Gershkovich talks to Annie Kelly about his arrest by the Russian intelligence services in 2023, his 16-month detention, and the swap deal that eventually took him home.Cartoon of the day | Tom GauldView image in fullscreen Illustration: Tom GauldThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenThreats to the puffin population can be mitigated. Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyIn this extract from his book The Puffin, Stephen Moss explains how for centuries, humans exploited puffins for food and ​feathers, but they have since become beloved symbols of wildlife.Sadly just as our national affection for them has grown, ​w​e are now endangering their future. Pollution and climate change are disrupting marine ecosystems, reducing key prey and making it harder for puffins to raise chicks.But there are reasons to be hopeful that we can turn the tide. Restricting industrial fishing, removing invasive predators and using advanced tracking technology can help us understand and therefore protect the humble puffin.As Moss says: “perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds.​”Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.
